item.title: REVIEW: Jackery HomePower 1000 Plus v2 Review: Pint-Sized Power Pack
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo
I’ve always hated gas generators. They’re noisy and heavy, they can be a pain in the ass to start, they fart out polluting fumes, and filling them usually involves a trip to the gas station. If I had to make a short list of great technology products that have come into their own in the last five years or so, high-capacity home backup batteries would be on it, because they free me from the tyranny of their gas-powered forebears. I’ve been trying out the $760 Jackery HomePower 1000 Plus v2, one of the latest in the company’s lineup of portable power packs. It’s a compact little box of energy that can crank out a steady 1,800W and features four three-prong AC outlets, two USB-C ports, one USB-A, and even a 12V lighter socket. It’s also super lightweight, at just under 24 pounds, and even has a nice swinging handle to help you carry it around. A compact, powerful-enough backup battery with plenty of ports. The 1000 Plus v2 is not totally perfect. It’s got a noisy, eager cooling fan, it takes a little doing to get it to recharge to full power, and it doesn’t have the full UL certification I’d like to see. But if you don’t need the larger batteries out there, it’s an ideal companion for camping trips, small power-tool use, and one-day outings where you need highly portable power. There’s no real setup for the HomePower 1000 Plus out of the box—you can start using it right away when you unpack it. (The unit I received arrived with a 28% battery charge.) You should still connect it to Jackery’s app, which just involves scanning for the device over Bluetooth, tapping its icon when it appears, then going through a brief setup that involves adding it to your Wi-Fi network, if you’d like. Once added to the app, the 1000 Plus v2’s home screen shows the battery’s current percentage and operating temperature, which ports are in use, and how many watts they’re outputting. This screen also contains basic controls like toggling ports on and off, activating the bright LED light on the device’s front, and flipping on the battery’s display. If your electric company offers a time-of-use (ToU) plan, you can use the 1000 Plus v2 to save a little money by diving into the app’s settings and configuring it to deliver power during peak hours (when energy costs more) and recharge when electricity is cheaper. When getting that ready, you can also enter your per-kWh prices for peak and off-peak hours. Back on the battery’s home page, you’ll then see an estimate of how much ToU mode has saved you. Another setting purportedly lets you limit the charging speed to anywhere between 100W and 1,800W. That’s a little confusing, since the device is actually limited to 1,600W recharging, according to its official specs. It also only climbed to (and stayed at) 1,060W when I first tested it; I had to turn on “Emergency Charging” in the app’s settings to reach 1,600W. I asked Jackery if the 1,800W option is a mistake or if there’s actually a way to reach that, and will update this story if it responds. Elsewhere in the settings, you can set some outlets to “priority” and others to “non-priority,” which tells the battery to shut off the latter when it reaches a level you set. That can be nice if you want to shut off other devices but keep a key appliance running as the battery wanes. The AC ports on other backup batteries I’ve tested—the DJI Power 2000 and the Anker Solix S2000—lack this kind of control and are either all on or all off. Most of the remaining settings focus on battery-saving measures, such as turning off Wi-Fi, turning off the battery if nothing has drawn power from it for a set period, and so on. These options are more or less the same ones that you’ll find on the Solix S2000, although the Jackery lacks any sort of analog to that device’s “Storm Guard” feature, which allows the battery to automatically recharge itself if the National Weather Service issues a storm warning for your area. That’s not a problem if you’re using the 1000 Plus v2 only as needed, but you could be left in a lurch if the power goes out after it’s been discharging all day during peak hours in ToU mode. Jackery packed a lot into this little guy, although things can get crowded—the four AC outlets are necessarily very close together, which could be an issue if you’re using large wall-wart-style plugs. Other than that, it’s all gravy: one of its USB-C ports outputs 140W, which is higher than the 100W you see on most 1kWh batteries. (The other is 30W.) And there’s a bright, circular LED that’s about the size of a quarter. It would be helpful when camping, although I could see the broad light strip on the front of the similar Anker Solix C1000 being even nicer. When using the HomePower 1000 Plus V2 around my apartment, I really appreciated its 24-pound weight, compact size, and swinging handle. It was easy to schlep from one room to the next, and its 12-inch-by-9-inch footprint is very forgiving in terms of placement. I started testing by checking how long the 1000 Plus v2 could last with its AC ports, display, and wireless connections active but nothing else drawing power. It lost 14% of its battery while running only the AC inverter for 24 hours. Just doing some back-of-the-envelope math, that’s an ambient loss of about 246Wh, or roughly 10W per hour, which is on the low end for 1kWh batteries like this. I also redid the refrigerator test I ran with the Solix S2000, which involved, well, plugging my fridge into the battery and seeing how long it could last with normal use. I found that I missed the S2000’s rear AC outlets, which let me hide the fridge’s cable in the back. Once I plugged the thing into the front, it ran for about 22.5 hours before the Jackery’s battery dropped to 3% and I switched the appliance back to the wall. That’s a little past the 19 hours quoted in a chart on the 1000 Plus’s product page, although my result is probably a best-case scenario because I don’t open my fridge more than three or four times in a day. The Solix S2000, which has twice the capacity, could power it about twice as long. Jackery’s specs mostly held up when I challenged them. Its AC ports handled higher wattages just fine; at a peak of over 1,700W, it seemed to keep going as long as it had the charge to run. If I exceeded 1,800W, as I did when I threw a hair dryer and a small space heater at it that pushed a combined 2,070W (well shy of the Jackery’s 3,600W peak surge capacity), the device ran both for about a minute until its AC output cut off and the Jackery app sent an AC output failure push notification on my phone. That was what I’d expected would happen, but all the same, it’s good to know you shouldn’t expect this battery to run a hair dryer and space heater simultaneously. It also shows that the 1000 Plus can clearly handle the initial surge required to start the motors of many smaller electric power tools. The 140W and 30W USB-C ports worked as expected, too. The battery hit 170W while powering an Anker Prime 300W power bank, which can simultaneously charge itself via its own dual USB-C ports. I particularly like that Jackery includes a 12V cigarette lighter DC port on this and other batteries, which handled the 100W my lightweight AstroAI portable air compressor requires just fine. It has always felt silly to turn on a whole car just to use this thing, and midwestern winters have made me wary of ever using my car’s battery for anything other than starting the engine. Using a compact battery is much more convenient. I wasn’t able to test the two DC8020 inputs on the battery’s side, which can accept up to 400W of solar charging from as many as four solar panels if you have a splitter that Jackery sells. It’s inconvenient that the company went with the DC8020 over other, more common ports used by most portable solar panels. As one reviewer at GearJunkie noted, that means you’re likely to need an adapter for third-party equipment, which just adds a point of failure. Jackery says it uses the DC8020 to bridge various connector standards, such as MC4 and XT60. I don’t have enough experience with solar power to have a strong opinion about this, except to say that my life has been better since most small tech moved to USB-C, and these various solar connector standards remind me of the bad times before that. Something I didn’t like about the HomePower 1000 Plus v2 was its fan noise. A degree of loud whirring is inevitable when you’re using a station, but Jackery’s is definitely louder than the only slightly larger Solix S2000. When I used it to power my TV and other devices in UPS mode, its fan periodically spun up loudly enough that I needed to turn the volume up a few clicks. That only happened when the battery was charging and discharging at the same time, though—in ToU mode or with the battery unplugged from the wall, it stayed quiet. On the plus side, the 1000 Plus v2 otherwise makes for a solid uninterruptible power supply, or UPS. Jackery says the machine can switch your devices from wall power to battery within 10 milliseconds. When I tested that claim by unplugging the 1000 Plus while playing games on my TV, I couldn’t tell the difference. If the 1000 Plus v2 unexpectedly loses wall power, you’ll get a push notification from the Jackery app, so you can find out about an outage even if you’re watching TV in complete darkness. Another plus is that the HomePower 1000 Plus v2 is expandable to 11kWh with Jackery’s $1,000 Battery Pack 2000 Plus v2, a stackable battery pack that adds an extra 2kWh of capacity. That’s quite a bit higher than similar portable 1kWh power stations like the EcoFlow Delta 3 Portable Power Station, which can only be expanded to 5kWh, or the Solix C1000, which has a max expansion of 2,112Wh. The Jackery HomePower 1000 Plus v2 is a great compact power station. Its 1,024Wh capacity makes it a solid option for backing up low-power appliances during power outages, and its 1,800W output is sufficient for many around-the-house, short-term use cases. Plus, its lightweight, roughly foot-wide body is a boon for placement around the house or packing for camping trips. My complaints about this device are few and mostly concern the absence of nice-to-haves. I wish it would charge itself if a storm is imminent, for instance, if I’m using it to save money on a ToU plan. The fan noise is also a bit much compared to that of other, larger 2kWh power stations I’ve tested, but it’s not disqualifyingly loud by any means. One reason not to buy the HomePower 1000 Plus v2 is its $760 price tag. While it does beat competitors on expandability, the EcoFlow Delta 3 and Anker Solix C1000 can both be had for $700 and $600, respectively, and each features six AC outlets rather than four (although three of the EcoFlow’s are two-prong). They may both be easier to justify, depending on what you’re after. But if being able to add more batteries later is a big deal to you, it’s hard to beat the compact, lightweight HomePower 1000 Plus v2.

item.title: REVIEW: Seagate One Touch 4TB external hard drive review
item.description:
Source: Latest from TechRadar US in News
As a standard portable 4TB HDD, this mechanical drive performs surprisingly well for backup and archieve, and if you want to use it as a working drive for lightweight video work, that’s perfectly possible. However, its real strength is the software Toolkit, which enables fast backups of all your computer files, plus strong password protection, all at a relatively reasonable price. Why you can trust TechRadar We spend hours testing every product or service we review, so you can be sure you're buying the best. Find out more about how we test. The Seagate One Touch 4TB is a relatively nondescript-looking portable HDD which is bus-powered directly through the USB-C data cable. The drive is relatively compact and slips easily into a laptop bag or pocket, making it highly portable. Whilst the exterior casing is mid-grey plastic, it’s nicely finished and feels robust. This portable drive features an HDD rather than an SSD, which does make this drive cheaper than some of the latest ultrafast drives I’ve looked at recently. Even so, at £179/US$199 at the time of writing this review, it’s still relatively expensive. For that money, you get the drive itself and a short 50cm USB-C cable to connect it to your machine. Getting started is easy: the drive comes formatted in exFAT, so it’s easily recognised on Mac, PC, and Linux systems. Opening on either iOS or Windows machines reveals free software that guides you through initial registration, downloads the Security Toolkit, and highlights partner deals Seagate has set up with Adobe, Synology, and Mylio. In this review, I’ve downloaded and installed the Toolkit, which is basically split into two parts. It includes a backup feature, which lets you choose different backup options for your computer and drive, and a security option, which lets you add a password and encrypt the drive’s contents. Alongside those software options, there are also partner deals, and all offer a limited trial period before you have to move to a full subscription. However, the Synology Deep Search is well worth mentioning. Whilst you only get six months of free use before needing to pay, if you need to manage multiple files and have a search feature driven by AI that is far better than your standard search options, especially on a Mac, then this really might be of interest. As a standard portable HDD, the 4TB capacity is perfect if you work with media files and need space for HD and 4K video. Whilst HDD technology limits speed, the benchmarking tests still showed impressive transfer rates, reaching over 140MB/s in some tests for both read and write. That transfer speed let me edit 4K footage shot on the GoPro Mission 1 ILS directly from the drive in Final Cut Pro X, and while the machine and drive occasionally had to catch up, editing a five-minute production was extremely smooth. Its real strength, however, is securely backing up your laptop or desktop data, and the included Toolkit software lets you run through a series of setup options with easy-to-follow prompts that work on both Mac and PC. Unlike many HDD and SSD portable drives that offer software encryption, this drive offers hardware AES 256-bit encryption that is managed through the Seagate Toolkit software. For my money, that makes it one of the best external hard drives for security. Through that software, you can encrypt the drive with a password lock. Because this security is hardware-based rather than software, it also meant that, through the benchmarking, when I tested the drive before and after the hardware encryption had been activated, the performance difference was minimal. It’s obvious from the aesthetics and material choices that this is a mid-range portable HDD, but the tests impressed me with its performance and overall quality. I'd definitely recommend it if you’re looking for a middle-of-the-road, no-frills, high-capacity HDD for general storage and backup, with the real value here being the Toolkit included with the drive. Seagate One Touch 4TB: Price and availability - Where can you get it? Directly from Seagate and online retailers. At present, the Seagate One Touch portable HDD is available in two different capacities - 2TB and 4TB, which retail for $160 and $200 respectively. In the UK, it's priced at £112 and £176. You can buy it direct from the Seagate website, where you'll also find a list of all stockists, which includes most major main online retailers. It comes in three colors: blue, grey, and white. Power: USB-powered, no external adapter required Security: Password protection and hardware encryption Lifting the drive from the box, and the 4TB version I’m looking at feels nice and tactile, with a wave surface texture that adds a little interest to the mid-grey colouring. The full build is plastic, yet it feels decent enough, with a single USB-C port at the back and, thankfully, a small white indicator LED right next to it. In terms of size and weight, it’s just a little larger than the compact 2.5-inch laptop-style HDD inside, with the casing measuring 115.3 × 80 × 20.9mm. The 4TB version I’ve looked at in this review weighs 268g. The USB-C cable is a bit longer than the ones I’ve seen with some other portable drives recently, measuring 50cm, which gives good reach to a desktop mini PC or laptop, depending on what you’re using. Whilst the One Touch name initially suggests fingerprint security, it actually refers to the company’s product line that offers one-click backup for your files. It also offers automatic backup folder mirroring and is plug-and-play, so the name really reflects how simple the drive is to use. Alongside the hardware comes a software suite, with installers on the drive's root that you can run once you plug it in. The drive comes pre-formatted in exFAT, but you can reformat it to match your native OS, Mac or PC. The software installer lets you install the files you need for the more advanced backup and security features, and I liked how streamlined the installation process was, with it guiding you through the initial setup step by step. The Seagate One Touch portable external hard drive is sold by the company as a premium portable, on-the-go backup solution, designed to be used equally in the home or out and about. This high-capacity portable hard drive comes with software options ready to install. These let you back up and secure your files, while software partnerships offer extended trial periods for apps to help you manage and organise files on the drive and on your host machine. The drive is available in three colour options: dark blue, space grey, and white. It’s also provided with a long USB-C cable, at 50cm, that runs from the drive to your host machine. This means your machine needs a USB-C port to work with this drive. The drive comes with bundled software, including the Seagate Toolkit, which requires registration but no other subscription costs. There’s also a two-month trial of Adobe Creative Cloud Pro, and six-month trials of Mylio and Synology Deep Search. You also get the superb Seagate Rescue Data Recovery Service. If the worst happens to your files, you can send the drive to Seagate, and they will see if they can recover anything that still exists. While this drive can be used as a portable working drive, Seagate has marketed this as a portable backup solution, and as such, it doesn’t highlight the transfer rate. However, with USB 3.2 Gen 1, essentially USB 3, you can expect a maximum theoretical bandwidth of 5Gbps, 625MB/s. However, since this contains an HDD, we can expect transfer rates between 120 and 150MB/s, which suggests Seagate matched the internal hardware and USB interface to maximise performance for its intended use as a portable backup rather than a working drive. CrystalDiskMark: Read 147.15MB/s; Write 146.06MB/s AJA System Test Lite: Read 132MB/s; Write 127MB/s ATTO Disk Benchmark: Read 133.55MB/s; Write 133.45MB/s AS SSD: Read 137.86MB/s; Write 130.28MB/s Getting started with the Seagate One Touch 4TB portable HDD is as easy as with any portable drive, and in this test, I used it on the MacBook Pro M1 Max and the HP EliteBook XG 21 laptop, along with a series of mini PCs. As I moved from macOS to Windows 11 Pro and Home, the Seagate One Touch performed similarly across all operating systems, which is great to see, and the simple USB-C connection was fully compatible with all the operating systems I tried. Because the drive came pre-formatted in exFAT, it was instantly recognised on both Mac and PC. I first installed the software on the MacBook Pro M1 Max to check out the backup options and security features, and I was impressed by how easy it was to set up. The initial stage requires you to register the drive and create a Seagate account, but once that’s done, it guides you through downloading the Seagate Toolkit installer, installing it, and then walking you through the setup options one after the other. For backup on the Mac, even though I have Time Machine activated, I selected a portion of my MacBook Pro’s hard drive, and once that initial setup was complete, the backup process started. What I like about the Toolkit is that it’s quick to access, and you can edit your backup plan at any time. Another point is that if you need to use the machine during a backup, as I did when I initially set up the plan, you can pause it so it doesn’t slow down your system, then restart it later. You can then schedule it to run overnight when you’re not using the machine. Likewise, on the PC, which doesn’t have such a sophisticated backup system as part of the OS, you can choose to mirror your mini PC, desktop, or laptop hard drive, and the registration and initiation process is just as easy. The second part of the included software is the security option, which uses AES 256-bit encryption and is activated through the Security Toolkit on both Mac and PC. It takes a little more setup, you need to enable certain security options and unplug and re-plug the drive for the installation to complete. But again, it’s extremely well documented, and the software guides you through every step, including adding an email address and phone number in case you forget the password you set. As backup software and an off-the-shelf, easy-to-use solution, this is as good as any paid option out there and is certainly easy to get your head around. Those two bits of bundled software really do balance the added cost of a standard 4TB portable HDD, and if you are looking for something cheaper, Seagate does make cheaper portable HDDs with this capacity. If you’re using this for business or your home office, I would highly recommend paying the extra for those security and backup features, since you’re only paying an extra $40 / £40 compared with the non-secure options. When it comes to performance, I used the drive for quick video editing in Final Cut Pro X and then CapCut, using files from the GoPro Mission 1 ILS. I was impressed by how fast this drive’s transfer rates were, both reading the files from the drive and writing the final render back to it during the test. I started with a simple HD edit, and even with footage shot in GoPro Log, it supplied and wrote data at the speed the system demanded. Even when I upgraded to 4K footage, it was still more than capable, with only the occasional pause as files were written. I’d still opt for an SSD over an HDD, but if you are caught out and need large-capacity storage on the move, then this will do the job. The only issue is that it doesn’t dissipate heat well, so it will thermal throttle during longer editing sessions. However, when I switched to editing stills shot on the Sony A7 IV and scans of Ilford FP4 Plus, the drive was more than capable of handling edits in DxO PhotoLab on the Mac and PC. As this drive is designed for archiving, it's a great option for small businesses looking for machine backup, photographers who want a solid, portable drive they can use in and out of the studio or anyone wanting a portable backup drive. The plastic exterior is lightweight, and it feels relatively robust. Plus, you can password-protect it for security. The Seagate One Touch 4TB portable HDD is a great all-round option for backup and a decent secure working drive for light media use. The design and build lean a bit toward plastic, but because it uses a single cable for power and data, you don’t have to carry a separate power supply, which makes it extremely convenient for field use. It’s clear this is designed as a backup drive rather than a working drive, and with HDD rather than SSD technology, transfer rates are slower. So if you are looking for a high-capacity working drive, this is perfectly capable, but you might want to look at an SSD option. This drive is marketed and better suited to backup and archive use, and the 4TB of capacity at this price is well balanced. What really sets this drive apart, and gives it an edge over many others, is its AES 256-bit hardware encryption, plus software that's exceptionally straightforward and easy to use. There’s just nothing complex about it. It does the job without going into any major complexities and offers excellent fallback when you need it. Whilst the aesthetics and build quality are very middle of the road, it’s all solid enough. After carrying the drive around for a week in my kit bag, it stood up to knocks and bashes without much issue, proving the plastic exterior is as robust as many metal options. If you are in the market for a high-capacity portable backup drive with hardware encryption and excellent bundled software, then I would highly recommend the Seagate One Touch 4TB HDD. It’s a well-balanced storage option without any aesthetic frills, with a main focus on pure functionality. Should I buy the Seagate One Touch 4TB? Buy it if... You need portable, high-capacity storage. This drive is built for high-capacity storage, with large internal drive options and a fast USB Type-C connection to your host machine. You want easy backup and security. The bundled software is about as good as I’ve seen for this type of portable HDD, offering easy backup and security in just a few clicks, with no complexity. Don't buy it if... You need high performance. While the HDD's performance is exceptionally good, its transfer rates are far slower than you’d expect from a standard SSD. You need physical and data security. While AES 256-bit hardware security gives you peace of mind that people won’t be able to access your files if you lose the drive, the physical design, while it will stand a knock or two, isn’t built as a tough, go-anywhere drive. item.title: REVIEW: Xiaomi 17T review: The most practical phone I’ve used in a while that’s also a rare bargain
item.description:
Source: Digital Trends
“Practicality with a little photographic punch”
- Excellent 5x periscope telephoto camera - Bright, smooth, vibrant AMOLED display Smartphones have become very good at convincing us that we need more. More cameras, more AI, more megapixels, more performance, more glass, more marketing slides about how the latest chip will change our lives. And then there’s the Xiaomi 17T, which makes a surprisingly convincing case for doing the basics exceptionally well. I’ve used the Xiaomi 17T as my primary phone for more than two months, including trips to Taiwan and Hawaii. It has handled everything from navigation and mobile data to photography, video recording, music streaming, messaging, and the occasional gaming session without making me think about switching to something else. The 6.59-inch display is bright and smooth, the speakers sound great, performance feels close to flagship territory in everyday use, and the 6,500mAh battery has been an absolute champ. The camera system is the icing on the cake, particularly the 50-megapixel periscope telephoto camera with its native 5x optical zoom. That said, it isn’t perfect. The design is a little too anonymous, the ultra-wide camera doesn’t always match the main camera’s colours, portrait separation can occasionally go wonky, and the selfie camera is fine rather than fabulous. HyperOS 3 is fluid and feature-rich, but definitely has room for improvement. Still, the Xiaomi 17T is the sort of phone that quietly makes life easier instead of constantly demanding attention. Xiaomi 17 specs: The nerdy bits, minus the nerdy lecture Note: We tested the Indian unit supplied by Xiaomi India. Specifications, network support, colour availability, and in-box accessories may vary by region. Design and build: Nice, but where’s the personality? Quick Take: Looks good, blends in, gets the job done. The Xiaomi 17T is a good-looking phone. Unfortunately, so are approximately seventeen other phones released this year. Okay, let me elaborate. See, there’s nothing especially wrong with its design. The flat display, clean rear panel, and relatively restrained camera island give it a modern appearance. At 200 grams and 8.17mm thick, it also avoids feeling like a chunky slab of glass and metal. Also, that blue finish on my review unit looks particularly premium, and the overall construction feels reassuringly solid. The problem is that the phone doesn’t have much of an identity. Put it on a table beside a handful of similarly priced Android phones, and it could easily disappear into the crowd. I’ve always appreciated phones that make a little effort to look different, and the Xiaomi 17T feels content to blend in. That’s a shame because the rest of the phone has considerably more character. Its 6.59-inch display strikes a lovely balance between screen real estate and handling comfort. I’m 6 feet 2 inches tall and have fairly large hands, yet the 17T feels like the sort of phone I can comfortably use without constantly readjusting my grip. That might not sound like a particularly exciting design achievement, but ergonomics are something people notice every single day. The display is flat, too, which gets a thumbs-up from me. Curved edges might look fancy in product photographs, but I’ll take a practical screen over unnecessary reflections and awkward edge touches any day. The phone has an IP68 rating for dust and water resistance and uses Corning Gorilla Glass 7i for display protection. There’s also an infrared blaster, allowing the phone to double as a remote for compatible TVs and other appliances. It’s one of those features that sounds like a gimmick until someone loses the actual remote. Then suddenly, the humble IR blaster is the hero of the household. The one obvious compromise, though, is the plastic frame. It doesn’t make the phone feel flimsy, but buyers spending this much may prefer the more premium materials used by some rivals. Still, I’d rather have a slightly less glamorous frame and a phone that’s comfortable to use than an unnecessarily heavy design that prioritises showroom appeal over everyday practicality. Display: Big, bright, and refreshingly sensible Quick Take: Bright, buttery-smooth, and easy on the eyes. The Xiaomi 17T’s 6.59-inch AMOLED display is one of its most consistently enjoyable features. It has a resolution of 2756 x 1268 pixels, a refresh rate of up to 120Hz, and support for Dolby Vision and HDR10+. The result is a sharp, colourful screen that makes everything from scrolling through social media to watching travel footage feel good. Colours are vibrant without being permanently locked into one look. Xiaomi offers display adjustments for people who prefer a more natural presentation, while those who enjoy punchier colours can tune things accordingly. The display also supports 12-bit colour output, and Xiaomi advertises peak brightness of up to 3,500 nits under specific conditions. It’s worth noting that that last number is a peak figure, not a brightness level the screen maintains across every app and situation. What matters more in everyday use, though, is that the display remains easy to read outdoors. I’ve had no significant trouble using it under bright sunlight, and its automatic brightness behaviour does a good job of adapting to changing conditions. Add to that, the 120Hz refresh rate makes scrolling and animations feel smooth, and I haven’t encountered any major issues that have interfered with daily use. The display also supports high-frequency PWM dimming and DC dimming, giving users options for managing screen flicker. I particularly appreciate the overall balance here. The screen is large enough for maps, videos, games, and multitasking, but the phone itself doesn’t feel absurdly oversized. It’s a very good display without the unnecessary theatrics. Performance: Almost flagship, without the flagship attitude Quick Take: Flagship-ish speed without the flagship-sized ego. The Xiaomi 17T is powered by MediaTek’s Dimensity 8500-Ultra, a 4nm chipset paired with 12GB of LPDDR5X RAM and UFS 4.1 storage. On paper, it might not sound as exciting as the silicon powering a full-blown flagship, but spend some time with the phone, and that distinction starts to feel a little academic. Apps open quickly, multitasking feels effortless, and jumping between navigation, WhatsApp, email, music, and the camera doesn’t leave me tapping the screen impatiently like I’m trying to summon a particularly lazy genie. What impresses me most is how consistently responsive the phone feels. After more than two months as my daily driver, I haven’t run into any major performance hiccups or frustrating stutters. It handles the usual assortment of everyday chaos without breaking a sweat, whether I’m checking directions, firing off messages, juggling apps, or quickly launching the camera to capture something before the moment disappears. The Xiaomi 17T doesn’t constantly remind me that it’s a step below a flagship. It just gets on with the job, which is precisely what a good phone should do. Gaming performance is solid, too, although I wouldn’t buy the 17T specifically to chase leaderboard-topping frame rates. I’ve played a few games on it, and the experience has been smooth, but I haven’t spent enough time running demanding titles through extended sessions to make sweeping claims about sustained frame rates or thermal throttling. The phone does get slightly warm during 4K video recording, but nothing I’ve encountered has raised a red flag. This is a capable all-rounder, not a gaming phone wearing a fake moustache and pretending to be something else. The benchmark results help put that experience into perspective. In 3DMark, the Xiaomi 17T scored 3,553 in Wild Life Extreme and 1,384 in Steel Nomad Light. These graphics tests push the GPU harder than everyday tasks do, giving us a better idea of how much headroom the phone has for demanding games and visually intensive workloads. For context, these scores put the 17T in the capable upper-midrange bracket, rather than alongside the most powerful gaming-focused flagships. I’ve also tested the Xiaomi 17T with Geekbench 7, so there’s an important caveat before comparing its results with scores from our other phone reviews. Geekbench 7 uses a different benchmark version, meaning its results aren’t directly comparable with Geekbench 6 scores. The phone recorded 1,130 in the single-core test and 3,591 in the multi-core test, offering a snapshot of its CPU performance without pretending that these numbers tell the whole story. And honestly, they don’t. Benchmarks are useful for establishing a baseline, but they can’t quite capture the feeling of using a phone for months without having to think about whether it’ll keep up. That’s ultimately where the Xiaomi 17T wins me over. It may not dominate benchmark charts, and buyers chasing maximum gaming performance will find more powerful options. But for everyday use, it feels remarkably close to flagship territory, with enough horsepower to handle the things most people actually do on their phones. Sometimes, the best performance feature is the one that doesn’t demand attention. The 17T has that down pat. Quick Take: That 5x zoom is doing some serious heavy lifting. The Xiaomi 17T has a triple rear camera setup comprising a 50MP main camera, a 50MP periscope telephoto with 5x optical zoom, and a 12MP ultra-wide. The Leica branding brings two distinct photographic styles, Authentic and Vibrant, along with the familiar colour tuning that gives Xiaomi photos their signature look. After using the phone across Taiwan and Hawaii, I came away impressed by how versatile the setup is. This isn’t just a phone that takes pretty pictures in perfect lighting; it’s one I was happy to rely on while travelling. The main camera is consistently dependable, the 5x telephoto is a genuine highlight, and even the ultra-wide has its moments. There are some familiar Xiaomi quirks, including a tendency to sharpen images a little too enthusiastically, and the cameras don’t always agree on colour. But those are caveats to an otherwise capable setup, rather than reasons to leave the phone behind when heading out to take pictures. The 50MP main camera is the workhorse here, and it rarely disappoints. Daylight shots are detailed, punchy, and full of contrast, with good dynamic range helping preserve detail in both bright skies and darker areas. Colours can look a little boosted, and fine details sometimes have that unmistakable Xiaomi oversharpening, but the results are generally pleasing without requiring much editing. It’s a camera that makes everyday scenes look interesting without needing a photography degree to operate. Low-light performance is equally reassuring. The camera does a good job balancing bright light sources with the surrounding shadows, rather than turning every night scene into an artificially bright mess. Details remain respectable, and noise is kept under control. I also prefer Leica Authentic when I want a more neutral starting point for edits or Instagram filters, although Leica Vibrant can look particularly appealing in tricky HDR scenes. Having both options is useful, and neither feels like a gimmick. The biggest reason to get excited about the Xiaomi 17T’s cameras is the 50MP periscope telephoto. A dedicated 5x optical zoom camera gives the phone a level of versatility that many otherwise capable phones lack. It lets me frame distant subjects without having to crop aggressively into a main-camera shot, and the results are impressively sharp. Whether I’m photographing architecture, distant details, or something across the street, 5x is a genuinely useful focal length rather than a spec-sheet party trick. Image quality at 5x is excellent in good lighting. There’s plenty of detail, colours look vibrant, and contrast gives photos a satisfying sense of depth. The longer focal length is also useful for portraits, creating a more natural-looking separation between the subject and the background. The catch is that portrait-mode edge detection isn’t completely consistent in my experience. It gets things right most of the time, but occasionally struggles around finer details. Think reliable most days, with the occasional bad hair day. The camera doesn’t fall apart once the light starts fading, either. Night shots at 5x retain a surprising amount of detail, and the phone does a good job of keeping noise from becoming too distracting. Sharpening becomes more noticeable in some situations, but the overall results remain very usable. Having a telephoto camera that can deliver respectable images after sunset makes the 17T more versatile than phones that treat zoom photography as a strictly daytime activity. Then there’s 10x zoom, which is honestly much better than I’d expect from a digital crop. Images can look impressively detailed at normal viewing sizes, and I haven’t found much to complain about unless I start pixel-peeping. Push the zoom further, and the compromises become more obvious, especially for anyone accustomed to the best flagship telephoto cameras. Still, most people aren’t going to inspect every photograph at 100% magnification. For everyday sharing and travel photography, the 17T gives users plenty of reach without immediately turning distant subjects into watercolours. The 12MP ultra-wide is useful when the main camera simply can’t fit everything into the frame. It works well for landscapes, architecture, and those occasions when stepping backwards isn’t an option. Daylight photos are generally detailed enough, with respectable dynamic range and controlled distortion. It’s not the most exciting camera on the phone, but it adds flexibility to a setup that already has a very capable main sensor and a proper telephoto. The biggest issue, at least in my testing, has been consistency. Colours can look noticeably different when switching between the ultra-wide and main cameras, which makes the transition less seamless than I’d like. Image quality also takes a hit in challenging lighting, where the smaller sensor has less room to work with. The ultra-wide remains perfectly usable, but it feels like the supporting cast next to two much stronger performers. The Xiaomi 17T can record up to 4K at 60 frames per second with both the main camera and the 5x telephoto, while the ultra-wide tops out at 4K at 30fps. Having high-resolution video across the rear cameras makes the setup genuinely useful for travel, where switching perspectives can make footage more interesting. I shot plenty of clips in Taiwan and Hawaii, and the results were detailed, colourful, and generally well exposed. The main and telephoto cameras are particularly dependable, with the 5x lens offering a useful way to capture distant scenes without sacrificing too much detail. Stabilisation also does a good job of keeping footage watchable while moving, although it isn’t completely immune to the occasional wobble. As with still photography, the cameras don’t always deliver identical colours, so switching lenses mid-shot can make differences more noticeable. Even so, the overall video experience is strong enough that I was comfortable using the 17T as my travel camera. Not every camera is a winner. Portrait-mode edge detection can be inconsistent, the ultra-wide doesn’t quite match the main camera for quality or colour, and the signature Xiaomi sharpening won’t appeal to everyone. The 32MP selfie camera is fine for casual photos and video calls, but it doesn’t excite me in the way selfie cameras from OPPO and Vivo often do. And even then, I still prefer the results I get from an iPhone. It gets the job done, but selfie enthusiasts may want more. Ultimately, though, the Xiaomi 17T has a camera system that punches above its weight, and its excellent 5x telephoto makes it far more versatile than a typical midrange phone. Battery life and charging: The phone that refuses to panic Quick Take: A battery that treats panic as a foreign concept. If the camera is my favourite thing about the Xiaomi 17T, its battery is a very close second. The 6,500mAh silicon-carbon cell delivers the kind of endurance that makes battery anxiety feel like someone else’s problem. My trips to Taiwan and Hawaii put it through the wringer: mobile data, navigation, music streaming, endless photos and videos, and even the occasional hotspot duty for my iPhone. This phone wasn’t enjoying a relaxing holiday. It was basically running a small travel agency, and it never once let me down. The 17T comfortably lasts a full day, even with the sort of heavy, gloriously unstructured use that comes with travelling. I’m talking maps while driving or walking, snapping photos, recording clips, replying to messages, and staying connected on mobile data. This isn’t a best-case scenario involving a few emails and three hours of scrolling. It’s the real-world chaos that usually sends lesser batteries looking for an emergency exit. When it’s finally time to plug in, Xiaomi’s 67W HyperCharge gets the job done, with support for up to 50W PPS charging using a compatible adapter. In my testing, a full charge takes roughly an hour. Sure, some Android rivals charge faster, but 67W is hardly crawling, especially when it’s replenishing a battery this large. Compared with the wired charging offered by many Apple, Samsung, and Google phones, it’s plenty quick. Wireless charging is missing, so anyone who relies on dropping a phone onto a charging pad may want to keep that in mind. Personally, I couldn’t care less; I’d rather have a battery that lasts all day than a fancy way to charge it while I’m asleep. The Xiaomi 17T delivers exactly that, without making me ration screen time or start scouting for wall sockets halfway through the afternoon. It’s a battery champ that just keeps going, and honestly, that’s a lot more useful than a flashy charging spec. Software and AI: Quietly capable, with one irritating quirk Quick Take: Less MIUI baggage, more getting on with life. The Xiaomi 17T runs Android 16 with HyperOS 3, and the software experience has been one of the pleasant surprises of using the phone for an extended period. HyperOS has a reputation that carries some baggage from the MIUI days, particularly around preinstalled apps and unnecessary clutter. The 17T feels considerably more restrained than that reputation might suggest. There are still preinstalled applications, but they haven’t overwhelmed my app drawer, and I don’t find myself constantly battling unwanted software. More importantly, the interface feels light and responsive. Animations are fluid, switching between apps is quick, and most of the features I want are already available without having to hunt for third-party alternatives. It doesn’t need to shout about itself. It simply gets on with the job. That’s not to say HyperOS is my favourite Android skin. I still prefer the overall experience of ColorOS, while Samsung’s One UI feels more premium to me. But the Xiaomi software has been dependable, and I appreciate the balance between a relatively clean experience and a broad set of built-in features. The infrared blaster is another example of a feature that makes the phone more practical than its marketing might suggest. Xiaomi’s remote-control app can operate compatible household devices, which is genuinely handy. The AI tools and integrations are there, including features tied to HyperOS and Google’s Gemini, but none has become a standout reason for me to use the phone. Xiaomi promises four generations of Android OS upgrades and six years of security updates for the 17T. That’s a useful commitment for anyone planning to keep the phone for several years, although the value of that promise will ultimately depend on how reliably updates arrive in practice. Quick Take: Surprisingly good sound, minus the tiny-phone embarrassment. The Xiaomi 17T’s stereo speakers have been excellent for the things I actually use them for: watching videos and listening to music. Audio is clear, the soundstage is enjoyable for a phone, and the speakers get loud enough to make casual listening comfortable without immediately turning everything into a tinny mess. The speakers are quite loud, clean, and generally well balanced, with limited distortion in the high frequencies. The phone also offers Dolby Atmos and other sound-enhancement options for users who want to tweak the output. I haven’t spent enough time gaming on the phone to offer a meaningful first-hand verdict on how its speakers perform during long gaming sessions. For video playback, music, and general everyday use, though, I have no complaints. They’re another example of the 17T getting an important part of the experience right without making a fuss about it. Should you buy the Xiaomi 17T? The Xiaomi 17T isn’t going to win any design awards, but spend a few weeks with it and that becomes a pretty minor complaint. The display is excellent, performance is smooth, the speakers sound great, and the battery could probably survive a small expedition. Then there’s the 5x telephoto camera, which gives this phone a genuinely useful trick up its sleeve. Much like the OnePlus 7T back in the day, this is a phone that gets the fundamentals right without needing to show off. Turns out, being good at almost everything is still a pretty great party trick. At the end of the day, you should consider buying the Xiaomi 17T if a great display, dependable battery life, smooth performance, and a versatile camera system matter more than flashy design or bragging rights. That said, skip it if flawless portrait shots, a top-tier selfie camera, premium materials, or brand prestige sit higher on the priority list. The compromises are real, but they’re hardly deal-breakers unless they happen to target the things that matter most. The Xiaomi 17T isn’t for everyone, and that’s fine. It’s for people who want a phone that makes everyday life easier, captures great travel photos, and doesn’t spend half the day begging for a charger. It may not make a grand entrance, but it absolutely delivers once the party gets going. If practicality is the priority, this phone makes a very convincing case for itself. The Samsung Galaxy S26 is the safer premium Android pick, with polished One UI software, long-term support, and a more established flagship experience. The Xiaomi 17T counters with a larger 6,500mAh battery and a dedicated 5x periscope camera, making it the more compelling option for travel photography and all-day endurance. The Google Pixel 11 makes a strong case for itself with Google’s clean Android experience, Gemini AI features, and clever computational photography tools. It also offers a premium build and seven years of software support. The Xiaomi 17T fights back with a larger battery, faster wired charging, and a versatile 5x periscope camera, making it a better fit for buyers who prioritise endurance and zoom photography over Google’s software smarts. The OnePlus 15R is the obvious alternative for buyers who prioritise raw performance, gaming, and fast charging. Its more powerful chipset and 80W charging give it an edge for demanding workloads and quick top-ups. The Xiaomi 17T counters with a dedicated 5x periscope camera and excellent battery life, making it the more versatile travel companion. OnePlus brings the horsepower; Xiaomi brings the zoom. I used the Xiaomi 17T as my primary phone for more than two months, including trips to Taiwan and Hawaii. My everyday use covered mobile data, navigation, photography, video recording, music streaming, messaging, email, and occasional gaming. Camera testing included daylight and low-light photography, portraits, ultra-wide shots, 5x optical zoom, higher zoom levels, and video recording with all three rear cameras. I also ran Geekbench 7 and 3DMark benchmarks to evaluate CPU and GPU performance. My battery observations reflect real-world use, including demanding travel days, rather than a controlled screen-on-time test. FAQs (Frequently Asked Questions) Is the Xiaomi 17T worth buying? Yes, the Xiaomi 17T is worth buying for its excellent 6.59-inch 120Hz AMOLED display, smooth everyday performance, dependable 6,500mAh battery, and versatile Leica camera system. Its 5x periscope telephoto camera is a particular highlight. However, the generic design, inconsistent portrait edge detection, and average selfie camera mean it isn’t perfect. It’s an excellent all-rounder for buyers who value practical features over flagship bragging rights. How good is the Xiaomi 17T camera? The Xiaomi 17T has a versatile Leica-tuned triple camera system with a 50MP main camera, a 50MP 5x periscope telephoto camera, and a 12MP ultra-wide camera. The main camera captures detailed photos in daylight and performs well in low light, while the 5x telephoto delivers impressive zoom shots. The ultra-wide is useful but less consistent with colours, and the 32MP selfie camera is competent rather than exceptional. How long does the Xiaomi 17T battery last? The Xiaomi 17T packs a 6,500mAh silicon-carbon battery that comfortably lasts a full day with heavy use. In my experience, it handles mobile data, navigation, music streaming, photography, video recording, and messaging without needing an emergency top-up. It supports 67W wired HyperCharge, although wireless charging isn’t available. Is the Xiaomi 17T good for gaming and everyday performance? Yes, the Xiaomi 17T delivers smooth everyday performance thanks to its MediaTek Dimensity 8500-Ultra processor, 12GB of RAM, and UFS 4.1 storage. Apps open quickly, multitasking feels effortless, and casual gaming is enjoyable. However, buyers seeking the highest possible frame rates or top-tier flagship gaming performance should consider more powerful alternatives. How long will the Xiaomi 17T receive Android and security updates? Xiaomi promises four generations of Android OS upgrades and six years of security updates for the Xiaomi 17T. The phone ships with Android 16 and HyperOS 3, giving buyers a feature-rich software experience with a substantial support window.

item.title: REVIEW: This Switch 2 sequel accessory was a few millimeters away from being good
item.description:
Source: The Verge
The Crkd Nitro Deck was a saving grace for the original Nintendo Switch. The slide-on $59.99 accessory brought Hall effect sticks to drift-plagued consoles — no need to open up your Joy-Con for a complicated repair. The Nitro Deck 2, made for both the original Switch and the larger Switch 2, continues the tradition of having better sticks than what Nintendo puts in even the newest Joy-Con (though these aren’t Hall effect or TMR). But it doesn’t feel as essential, and there’s one thing I really can’t stand about it. This Switch 2 sequel accessory was a few millimeters away from being good Crkd’s $99.99 Nitro Deck 2 has some improvements, with Switch and Switch 2 compatibility, but it’s far from essential. If you buy something from a link, The Verge may earn a commission. See our ethics statement. It’s too difficult to use the Nitro Deck 2’s ABXY face buttons without the right stick getting in the way. The stick-to-button arrangement is a big step down from the original Nitro Deck (and especially bad compared with the symmetrical Steam Deck-like stick layout in the video output-ready Nitro Deck Plus). I’m surprised Crkd’s team thought this was an improvement. My patience with the run-based gameplay in Echo Weaver is already tested enough, and trying to quickly hammer inputs on the Deck 2 only adds to the frustration. Your preference may differ, but I like having a little breathing room between the right stick and the face buttons. Some companies choose to space them out or, in the case of the Switch 2’s Joy-Con, make the stick small enough to allow my thumb to hover over it so I can press the buttons. The Deck 2 makes me adjust my thumb’s angle of approach outside of what’s comfortable. It’s just a few millimeters off. The original’s superior slide-in design was traded for a vice-grip design to ensure compatibility with both the newer and older Switch consoles. The Deck 2 has a twisting mechanism on the back that you can loosen, tighten, or lock. It’s clever, though the tradeoff for broader compatibility is a design that feels inherently less secure. Crkd is asking Switch 2 owners to put a ton of faith in this mechanism staying tight around their $500 consoles. My Switch 2 didn’t feel wobbly during testing, but I’d rather not have to think about its safety at all when I’m gaming. I would have preferred a slide-in design for the Deck 2 made expressly for the Switch 2. It’s disappointing that Crkd’s Joy-Con-replacing solution isn’t as good because I like some things about it more than the original. For instance, the accessory has adjustable tension on both sticks, so they can snap back to their original position faster or slower than the default speed. Also, the accessory’s bulkier design makes the console more comfortable in my medium-size hands to use in handheld mode. It also has a bunch of customizable buttons: four on its back and an extra near the triggers. Not many similar accessories are out there yet, and the other one I tried (the abxylute N6) wasn’t all that good, either. I plan to test Mobapad’s latest take on Joy-Con soon, and it seems promising. Alternatively, you can add a bunch of comfort to your Switch 2 in handheld mode with either the Dbrand Killswitch 2 or the Mechanism Basecase. And with the money left over, you could buy a good wireless Switch 2 controller with long-lasting sticks and better rumble. Photography by Cameron Faulkner / The Verge

item.title: REVIEW: Beelink ME Pro Creator Edition NAS review
item.description:
Source: Latest from TechRadar US in News
It’s wonderful to see Beelink being so bullish about NAS, and coming to market with such developed solutions. This product shows off great build quality, modularity, performance and innovation in one relatively affordable package. Beelink deserves some praise for this hardware and software combo. Why you can trust TechRadar We spend hours testing every product or service we review, so you can be sure you're buying the best. Find out more about how we test. Beelink ME Pro Creator Edition: 30-second review This review covers the four-bay ‘Creator NAS’ as Beelink calls it, which is available in two SKUs and uses the Intel Core i5-13500H mobile processor. But Beelink has five ‘Home NAS’ options below that one, using the Intel J5005, N95, N150 and Core 304 processors. And another two higher-end options with AMD Ryzen AI 350 and AI 470 class processors. The four-bay enclosure is a compact all-metal unibody, measuring 165 x 121 x 185mm and weighing 2.4kg without drives. Beelink says it is 50 per cent smaller in volume than a conventional design, and compared to anything by Synology or QNAP, it’s certainly much smaller. Inside, an internal blower on the motherboard module pulls cool air in and pushes it out to keep everything cool, and the milled aluminium construction also helps radiate heat. Silicone mounts sit either side of each drive and between the case and the motherboard tray, reducing vibration and noise The review unit, with its Intel Core i5 13500H, has 12 cores, 16 threads and a 45W TDP. It comes with 32GB of DDR4, a 500GB system SSD and four M.2 slots. Beelink pitches it at creative professionals, and this is a great spec for those who need large amounts of fast storage for video editing or maintaining photo collections. Earlier Beelink NAS used the FygoOS operating system, and it’s also in this NAS. It is flexible and well-featured, and it makes the ME Pro feel like a platform rather than an appliance. The evolution of this aspect is impressive, and FygoOS delivers many of the higher-end features that some NAS products lack. However, there is one caveat. This is a Kickstarter launch product; therefore, a pledge is not a purchase, and delivery dates can slip. Buyers need to weigh that, but so far I’m impressed with this NAS on several critical levels. And if the Kickstarter goes well and this hardware ends up in the retail channel, it might be included in our best NAS devices. Beelink ME Pro Creator Edition: Price and availability - Where can you get it? Only on Kickstarter initially The ME Pro range is listed as coming soon on Kickstarter. Beelink is offering a Super Early Bird discount of 30 per cent. Prices are in US dollars, and drives are not included. The 13500H four-bay costs $819 at Super Early Bird and $1,169 at list. All four-bay prices are below, Super Early Bird first, then list. A $10 VIP deposit before launch unlocks a free four-bay upgrade. And if you back the two-bay tier machine, you will receive the four-bay model at the same price. Given what some of these designs include in processing power and memory, these are mostly excellent deals. Specifically, $819 for the Creator NAS seems like exceptional value. The drawer-style design is a neat idea: it uses almost the same mechanism as the drives, but replicated on the motherboard, which slides out for maintenance and upgrades. That should make a processor upgrade a far simpler job than in a normal NAS. Beelink has also hinted at AMD and ARM boards in the same chassis. If you own a four-bay, you could buy a different two-bay and swap the platforms, in theory. The unibody metal case is milled from solid aluminium and makes for a small footprint for a four-bay NAS. It’s also quiet enough that this could sit on a desktop. Cooling relies on one internal blower rather than a bank of case fans, and when the motherboard module is removed, the dual-sided design is clearly influenced by Beelink’s mini PC designs. Access to the two M.2 2280 Gen4 slots is super-simple, and they come with their own chunky heatsinks to help remove heat with the help of the fan assembly. There are two other M.2 slots (Gen 3 x2), one of these being occupied by the FygoOS installation, but getting those requires removing the fan. Since the unused third slot doesn’t run at the same speed as the two easily accessible ones, it probably wouldn’t be a good plan to try to make a RAID array of the three, but that slot might be useful for a caching SSD. What I’m less impressed with is that the trays aren't tool-less for either 3.5- or 2.5-inch mechanisms. Each drive needs four screws, and once installed, two more hold it in place from the back of the tray. The designers' issue here was that if they used a tool-less tray and a more elegant lock, then the NAS would be bigger, and the designers didn’t care for that. They also used four of these tiny screws to hold the motherboard tray in place, and these screws are easy to misplace. One annoyance is that, to hold the thin steel air filter on the rear of the NAS, ten small magnets are glued into the chassis. They are placed within 4mm of where the screws hold the trays in, which inevitably means that when you go to screw them in, the magnets pull the screw off the screwdriver before you can thread it. In short, the filter didn’t need that many magnets, and they didn’t need to be where the tray screws are. The fine irony of all these screws is that the enclosure tolerances are so good that the screws holding the trays in and the motherboard are mostly pointless, certainly with the numbers used. These points aside, the ME Pro is better built than most NAS enclosures, even if some compromises have been made to keep it so small. Beelink ME Pro Creator Edition: Features As a laptop processor, the Core 5 13500H was a strong platform sporting 12 cores total (4 Performance-cores with Hyper-Threading and 8 Efficient-cores) and 16 threads. As is the way with Intel 13th Gen technology, the performance-cores boost at a higher level, up to 4.7 GHz; and the efficient-cores boost at lower levels, up to 3.5 GHz. All cores share an 18 MB Intel Smart Cache, and the chip has a base power TDP of 45W. Some laptop designs using this chip scaled power up to 115W, but from what I understand, the ME Pro has more than enough performance at its base wattage. The review hardware came with two 16GB DDR4-3200 modules providing 32GB, but if you can find them, this system could take dual 48GB modules for 96GB in total. It’s a shame Beelink didn’t use LPDDR5 for faster performance and lower power consumption, but the cost was probably prohibitive when these decisions were made. The GPU is an Intel Iris Xe Graphics with 80 execution units running up to 1.45 GHz, and it shares memory with the rest of the platform. The best aspect of this processor, aside from its high core count, is its PCIe lanes: 28 total. In this design, not all 28 lanes are created equal. Eight primary lanes are Gen5, eight secondary lanes are Gen4, and all sixteen lanes are CPU-attached. The final twelve lanes route through the Platform Controller Hub (PCH) to handle slower or secondary peripherals (like Wi-Fi/Bluetooth, audio controllers, USB extensions, or secondary M.2 storage slots), and these are all Gen3. That’s a terrific amount of bandwidth, and it enables dual M.2 Gen 4 x4, two more M.2 Gen3, a 10GbE LAN port and a 2.5GbE LAN port, a Thunderbolt 4 port, and three USB 3.2 Gen2 ports. That’s plenty for most people, as you can use the Thunderbolt port as a 40Gbps network connection if needed. Overall, the architecture choices in this NAS are right for demanding workloads like video editing, photo manipulation, and software development, thanks to its hybrid core layout. However, only the Ryzen AI models are sold specifically for local language models. The 13500H review unit is not one of them, and Beelink lists no AI performance figure for it. The AI 470 is quoted at up to 86 TOPS, with that number assembled from an NPU with 55 TOPS and a CPU and GPU combined for 32 TOPS. Therefore, if you intend to run AI models on the NAS, one of the AMD machines would be preferable to this system. Beelink ME Pro Creator Edition: Software FygoOS is the international face of a Chinese NAS solution that has surfaced in the past year. Its parent is fnOS, also called Feiniu Private Cloud. I believe a small team of NAS enthusiasts built it around Debian Linux, and it is closed source. During its public beta, it was offered as a free option for Chinese home users. Reviews for this platform only began in early July 2026. Early adopters found a new NAS OS in version 1.2 and the FygoTV app in 0.9. The name hints at open source, but it is a proprietary system built partly on open source parts, with GPL source releases still in progress. It runs on x86 and ARM hardware and offers ZFS, Btrfs and ext4 storage. The changelog shows active development. During my time with the ME Pro 4, it had several releases; I used version 1.2.0800, and FygoTV was 0.9.7-3. FygoOS is the beating heart of the ME Pro, and it aims at beginners while leaving room for experts. Beelink says apps install with one click and update the same way. It lists official and community apps for media, backup, productivity and virtualisation. For what appears to be a relatively new NAS OS, this all seems much more advanced than I’d normally expect, both in application selection and feature set. As far as I’m aware, FygoOS is the only other hardware-included NAS OS with ZFS file system support other than QNAP QuTS hero. You can get this feature via Unraid, TrueNAS or OpenMediaVault, among other places, but you would be installing them onto this hardware to replace FygoOS. Included in the selection of apps is a powerful photo and media search tool. It can use AI to rapidly find images using facial recognition and smart categorisation. The private cinema feature matches metadata automatically, and Beelink claims up to 99 per cent accuracy in identifying the content. It also syncs playback between devices and supports real-time hardware transcoding. However, I was disappointed that, as nice as some of these tools are, Beelink missed a few tricks. One is the HDMI port, which is promoted as supporting up to 4K output. That might be true, but it can’t be driven by the Fygo TV app to play files directly onto a TV. That’s something you can do with a Ugreen or Asustor NAS, but not this. But there are a few things it can do that are more exclusive. One of the more surprising features of this platform is the collaborative media workspace. Teams can preview video, photos, audio, documents, fonts and 3D files without downloading them. AI search finds content by meaning, not just file names. You can send a review link, and reviewers add comments, annotations and timestamped notes. Sharing supports access controls, expiry dates, watermarks and branding. The only caveat is that the features are tiered, with the best ones requiring a subscription. The personal tier is included in all ME Pro. The business tier comes with a 30-day free trial on the J5005, N95, N150 and 304 models. The 13500H and both Ryzen AI models get six months free. But, and this is a concern, Beelink has not said what the business tier costs afterwards. I’d hate to use this for six months, find it incredibly useful and then discover that the monthly cost is too high to make it practical. Being an Intel-based platform, and not ARM, this NAS supports virtualisation and with 32GB of RAM it is relatively easy to have several VT instances running. And, it has Docker, expanding the amount of software that can run on this platform dramatically. It was interesting to note that while the hardware used here, specifically the Core i5 13500H, doesn’t have an NPU, it is a reasonably powerful processor and it has Iris Xe graphics, which can be used to process AI LLMs. The standard application set includes Ollama, and I was able to install it and use it to run a local model like Gemma. While it wasn’t the fastest response, it did work quite well, so using this machine for AI isn’t impossible. Obviously, if you want to use the NAS as an AI assistant, the two models with AMD Ryzen AI processors are a better choice, but even without a dedicated NPU, this hardware can run some AI and support interactive chats without relying on the Cloud. Beelink ME Pro Creator Edition: Performance When I started testing this NAS, I soon realised the platform was largely twiddling its thumbs during large file transfers. Using the 2.5GbE LAN port, no SSD cache and four 4TB drives in a RAID 5 pack, the CPU barely hit 9% usage. And that was shipping a file from my desktop PC at around 290MB/s. Using the 10GbE port increased transfer speeds to nearly 700MB/s, but only added a few percentage points of CPU overhead. With an SSD, this machine can get closer to 1000MB/s, either directly or by allocating the SSD for reading and writing cache. Four 3.5-inch drives don’t have enough performance to fully saturate the 10GbE link without cache support, so adding an SSD is more of a necessity if you're involved in file serving. Gen4 x4 M.2 slots are great for internal SSD performance, but there aren’t many practical ways to use that bandwidth from the outside other than the Thunderbolt 4 port. But unfortunately, the Thunderbolt port on this NAS doesn’t yet support Host mode, even though it is listed as a feature that’s ‘under development’ on the official FygoOS roadmap. Also, while the networking functions enable Multi-gateway mode, where the LAN ports route according to the shortest path to the target system, there is currently no link aggregation/channel bonding. I don’t think channel bonding a 10GbE and a 2.5GbE line together is a good idea anyway, but FygoOS currently doesn’t have the necessary interfaces for this. Because FygoOS is built on a Linux base, users looking to combine multiple network interfaces typically have to configure network bonding manually via SSH or underlying Linux networking tools rather than a native settings panel. On a more positive note, I used a cheap Ugreen USB-A to 2.5GbE LAN port (CM648), and that worked perfectly for what is an incredibly inexpensive option. I know that Ugreen makes a 5GbE version of this adapter, and I suspect that would also be useful in this context. Ideally, this system would have dual 10GbE and SMB multi-channel mode, but in most other respects, this NAS is overpowered for most roles. Beelink ME Pro Creator Edition: Final verdict Buy it if you want a compact NAS that you can upgrade later and you like the idea of a modern, flexible OS. Beelink pitches the 13500H model to creative professionals, and it has the core count to back it up. That said, the four-bay market is crowded. Alternatives include the Ugreen NASync DXP4800 Plus and Pro, the Synology DS925+ and the UniFi UNAS Pro 4. Breaking down the ups and downs of each design would take another article, but to cover the basics, none of them matches the ME Pro 4-Bay Creator Edition. The Ugreen NAS units are cheaper, use DDR5 and include special features like SMB Multichannel and HDMI video playback, which makes them useful. Synology’s DS925+ uses a much weaker AMD Ryzen V1500B quad-core CPU, only has dual 2.5GbE LAN ports, comes with 4GB of RAM expandable to 32GB, and has two M.2 slots that can only use Synology-branded storage. That machine supports ECC memory, but that and the DSM OS are the only real positives. The UniFi UNAS Pro 4 is meant for racks, not shelves, and is an ARM SoC system that supports four HDDs, two M.2 NVMe SSDs, and 2x 10Gb SFP+ LAN ports. It’s cheap, around $600, but the 8GB memory can’t be upgraded, and the ARM architecture doesn’t support Virtual Machines. What I haven't considered are the Asustor Lockerstor 4 models, QNAP, and TerraMaster options, to name a few. But to generalise, most 4-bay NAS don’t compete on processing power, memory capacity, and build quality. The fly in this ointment is that until this product exits the Kickstarter campaign and people have them longer term, will they be able to establish a reputation, good or bad. I haven't had any issues with the machine Beelink sent, and with a few more updates to FygoOS, it could become a useful NAS to own. But for those who have had bad Kickstarter experiences, wait if you need proven reliability. This is a new product on a crowdfunding platform, and the modular upgrade path is so far a promise. But as a first-generation device, the Beelink ME Pro Creator Edition is certainly heading in the right direction. Should you buy a Beelink ME Pro Creator Edition? Buy it if... With one 10GbE LAN and the 2.5GbE Port as a failover backup, you can distribute 1000MB/s of data over a network easily. And, using the USB or Thunderbolt port, you can get even more network bandwidth. Being able to scale to 96GB of memory enables this NAS to handle jobs that would overrun other devices. It’s also DDR4, which might be cheaper to find than DDR5 at this time. Don't buy it if... While this machine can run an LLM, the lack of an NPU in the processor holds it back, and you can’t add a powerful GPU, as it doesn’t have OCuLink. If you want AI on a NAS, other machines in this range are better suited. With this system having a Thunderbolt port, I was hoping it would have host mode, enabling a suitable laptop to link directly to the NAS with a 40Gbps link. However, that feature is still to be added to FygoOS, and until it is, that remains a pipe dream. For more NAS solutions we've collated the best NAS hard drives around
