item.title: REVIEW: LG UltraGear evo GX9 Review: Tandem OLED Shines in This Brutalist Gaming Monitor
item.description:
Source: PCMag
The LG UltraGear evo GX9 ($1,799.99) is a 39-inch ultrawide curved gaming monitor with a lot going for it. It’s the world’s first so-called "5K2K" (5,120-by-2,160-pixel) OLED gaming monitor of its screen size, and it's based on LG’s fourth-gen Primary RGB Tandem QD-OLED panel. It’s an impressive screen, with a wide enough wingspan to support multiple windows and various productivity workflows, as well as some high-end gaming, of course. Its AI features likely drive up the price and made a few missteps, though. The slightly bigger but AI-free LG 45 Ultragear OLED (45GX950A-B) and the 39-inch Alienware 39 5K OLED Gaming Monitor (AW3926QW) are better choices and remain our Editors' Choice picks in this category. The UltraGear evo GX9 uses LG's latest generation of its Primary RGB Penta Tandem OLED technology, referred to as a “Primary RGB Tandem”. This new panel technology addresses common pain points that affected previous QD-OLED panels, such as low brightness, blurry text, and lackluster black-level performance under high ambient light. We’ve seen similar technologies appear in some of this year’s OLED monitor releases. The Alienware 34 280Hz QD-OLED (AW3426DW) offers a similar upgrade, courtesy of Samsung, albeit under a different name: QD-OLED Penta Tandem. A close look reveals its makeup is similar to that of LG's Tandem RGB QD-OLED. Both include DisplayHDR TrueBlack 500 certification and a rated peak HDR brightness of 1,300 nits. (And by the way, in case it's not clear from the above discussion, Samsung and LG make the panels that go into most gaming monitors, from Alienware to Zowie.) The UltraGear evo GX9 has a 21:9 aspect ratio and a 1500R curve, which stands for 1,500mm—the radius of a circle formed by a hypothetical ring of these monitors placed edge to edge. Bigger screens tend to have tighter curves. Probably the most interesting thing about the monitor to me, aside from its new panel tech, is its built-in processor. While LG doesn’t disclose the specific model name, core architecture, or processor brand, the company claims it uses AI upscaling to enhance lower-resolution content to fit the display’s 5K2K resolution. To be clear, the monitor's native resolution is still 5K2K, but this optional feature is supposed to help consoles and low-end computers, which output at lower peak resolutions, experience the full effect of the screen. On paper, this AI upscaling seems similar to upscaling technologies such as AMD FSR and Nvidia DLSS, but it's handled by the monitor's processor and not your computer's GPU. We’ll see how that plays out in the game performance section below, but first, let's take a look at the rest of what the monitor has to offer. The back of the cabinet has a simple, matte-black finish without any loud logos. The only indication that it’s a gaming monitor is the UltraGear branding along the stand. The hexagon shape on the back houses the monitor’s RGB lighting, which can be controlled from the on-screen display (OSD). Also on the back, you’ll find a row of ports: two HDMI 2.1 connectors, a DisplayPort 2.1 jack, two USB Type-A ports (version 3.2 Gen 2), a USB Type-C jack with 90 watts of power delivery, and a headphone jack. Overall, it’s a brutalist-look design, with a thick base, stand, and chassis. It measures 23.8 by 36.3 by 12.7 inches with the stand fully extended, and it weighs 23.6 pounds. Other features include two built-in 7-watt stereo speakers, into which LG also worked an AI-powered feature. Called AI Sound, it separates individual audio elements to create a more controlled and more immersive sound profile, LG claims. I put this to the test with King Krule's "Pink Shell," a bass-heavy song that I like to use to test speakers on monitors and laptops. The built-in speakers do sound loud, though they lack the hard-hitting bass you'd get from external computer speakers. Even with the bass boost enabled, the song's heavy bass notes didn't feel any richer. To my ear, AI Sound noticeably cleans up the sound and makes it easier to identify different parts of the track, but doesn't really improve the overall listening experience. It also seems to add reverb that isn’t in the original song. For gamers not interested in AI-powered audio, the UltraGear has plenty of other features to recommend it. The most useful is certainly the dual-mode capability, which supports different peak refresh rates at two resolutions: 165Hz at the native 5,120-by-2,160 resolution, and 330Hz at a lower 2,560-by-1,080 resolution. You can also shrink the effective display area to 34, 27, or 24.5 inches, masking out part of the screen around the image. This might better cater to your needs if you're a hard-core gamer who prefers smaller screen areas for competitive play but still enjoys the expansive experience of an ultrawide on more immersive titles or when not gaming. The next step in our evaluation: putting the monitor through our standard benchmark tests using Portrait Displays' Calman calibration software and a Klein K-10A colorimeter. I also ran it through a gauntlet of games to measure input lag and judge its real-world performance. (I took these readings with out-of-the-box settings, unless otherwise noted.) In the first test, I benchmarked the display brightness using the out-of-the-box SDR profile. Under these conditions, I measured 322 nits at a 10% window size, right between LG's listed typical brightness of 330 nits and its minimum of 300 nits. Moving on to HDR, the monitor promises a peak HDR brightness of 1,500 nits at 1.5% average picture level (APL). APL is defined by how much of the image you’re displaying is bright and how much of it is dark, so by changing the window-size presets in Calman, we can alter the APL of the image being measured. Typically, this is represented by differently sized white windows as measured against a black background. For example, at a 25% window size, the white box occupies a quarter of the black background, thus simulating 25% APL. Reducing the window size to 2% (there is no 1.5% preset), I measured 1,235 nits of brightness. LG also suggests that typical HDR brightness should hit 600 nits at a 10% APL, and I recorded 541 nits at a 10% window size. That's under 600 nits, but more in line with its VESA DisplayHDR True Black 500 rating. Either way, although the test results did not quite nail LG's HDR targets, I thought the HDR application looked good. The LG UltraGear evo GX9 is rated for a dynamic contrast ratio of 1,850,000:1, slightly higher than recent OLED monitors, including the Alienware AW3926QW, Alienware 34 280Hz QD-OLED (AW3426DW), and the Asus ROG PG34WCDN. That sky-high figure indicates the display's ability to produce deep blacks alongside bright whites, resulting in stellar quality in both light and dark scenes. Most non-OLED monitors have rated contrast ratios of 2,000:1 or less. Compared with them, OLEDs offer essentially infinite contrast ratios, making the eight-digit ratios really just number soup. This is true of both premium and entry-level OLED gaming monitors. Also in Calman, I tested the color gamut. My metering indicates that the LG UltraGear evo GX9 covers 98.3% of the Adobe RGB color space, 151% of the sRGB color space, and 99.5% of the DCI-P3 color space. The charts above and below show the Adobe RGB and DCI-P3 results, respectively. The squares represent target color reference points, and the circles represent the actual measured color. The panel exceeds 100% sRGB, as many OLED monitors do, which can occasionally result in an overblown image. Still, the wider gamut can result in richer colors, especially when viewing HDR content. Moving on to input lag testing, I used the Leo Bodnar 4K Input Lag Tester to measure the UltraGear evo GX9’s input lag times across various combinations of refresh rates and resolutions. Low input lag is critical for hard-core gaming and esports, but you can benefit from it even if you're a casual gamer. I started my input-lag tests at full HD (1080p). At 1080p/60Hz, I recorded 9.5ms of input lag, and at 1080p/120Hz, 4.8ms. At 1080p/240Hz, the measurement was a stellar 3.1ms. At QHD (1440p) resolution, the monitor recorded 6.6ms of input lag at 60Hz and 9.3ms at 120Hz. Finally, at 4K/60Hz, I recorded 9.2 ms of input lag. (The Bodnar device can't measure above 120Hz at 1440p, or above 240Hz at 1080p.) Ultrawide gaming is no longer a niche, as many games now support wider aspect ratios. In my testing, I tried Cyberpunk 2077, Doom: The Dark Ages, and Pragmata on this panel, all of which support ultrawide aspect ratios, high frame rates, and HDR. And they all looked good, too. The monitor supports AMD FreeSync Premium Pro and is Nvidia G-Sync Compatible, which should eliminate screen tearing, blur, and ghosting. I also tested the AI upscaling feature and found a lot of variables to consider. On the monitor's product page, LG notes that the input source must be at least "Wide Full HD" (2,560 by 1,080 pixels; lower resolutions are not supported), though LG suggested to me that 1,920 by 1,080p at 60Hz is where you want to be. The monitor's settings offer two upscaling options: High and Low. For PC users, the tricky part, surprisingly, is setting your computer's active signal to 1,920 by 1,080 pixels. To do this, you must navigate to the Adaptive Properties setting in Windows (System > Display > Advanced Display > Adaptive Properties) and set the screen's resolution to 1,920 by 1,080 pixels at 60Hz. Ensure that the display is the only display detected, then double-check the active signal resolution in the monitor's OSD by navigating to General > Information. With computer settings verified, I loaded up Cyberpunk 2077, expecting to see a huge jump in screen resolution and...I didn't. I toggled the monitor's AI upscaling on and off in different locations to see if a difference emerged, but I saw none. As it turns out, it was a simple fix: You need to be on the 5K2K/165Hz mode, too. With that sorted, I finally saw the upscaling in action. On Pragmata's title screen, for example, the difference in the face of the main character, Diana, was obvious. The sharpening was evident, but on the High setting, the characters looked a little, well, "deep-fried." In action scenes, the high contrast did clean up distant objects, but the effect wasn't overly noticeable in the foreground. While the High setting showed the more obvious change, the Low setting produced a more pleasing image to my eyes. Ultimately, though, neither looked particularly good; I preferred the softness of the native image. I jumped among Cyberpunk 2077, Doom: The Dark Ages, and Marvel Rivals, and the results were similar. At best, the image looked over-sharpened. At worst, I saw little change at all. To me, the trouble isn't really worth the reward, and if you're shelling out money for a 5K2K monitor, chances are your GPU is better at upscaling, anyway. You'll jump through fewer hoops upscaling from a console. In fact, LG showcases the technology by upscaling The Legend of Zelda: Breath of the Wild on the Nintendo Switch (which has a max resolution of 1080p). Whether you're playing on a current console or a last-gen one, you can manually adjust your console's output resolution in its system settings. Set the console's resolution to 1080p/60Hz and rely on the monitor's upscaling, and you'll find it noticeably sharpens and upscales a 1080p image to 4K. I confirmed this with the Xbox One using Fortnite. But like on the PC, this crunchier image isn't really worth the trouble. The AI upscaling feature actually does work, but it's hard to recommend playing consoles on an ultrawide monitor anyway, as they don't natively support 21:9 aspect ratios and certainly don't support the UltraGear evo GX9's 5K native resolution. There's also no practical reason to lower the resolution of a 4K source to 1080p, only to upscale it to 4K again, when you could just set your console to 4K in the first place. It may prove more useful for older consoles that output at 1080p/60Hz, like the original Nintendo Switch or even something older like a PlayStation 3, but that's an edge case—no one should be buying this monitor to use primarily with a vintage console. LG advertises upscaling as a selling point, but the fact that it only works under very specific circumstances (and when it does, it's not game-changing) makes me wonder why the feature is here at all. You can just ignore it, but I would prefer it to be omitted entirely if that meant a lower price for this otherwise excellent monitor. - 5.0 - Exemplary: Near perfection, ground-breaking - 4.5 - Outstanding: Best in class, acts as a benchmark for measuring competitors - 4.0 - Excellent: A performance, feature, or value leader in its class, with few shortfalls - 3.5 - Good: Does what the product should do, and does so better than many competitors - 3.0 - Average: Does what the product should do, and sits in the middle of the pack - 2.5 - Fair: We have some reservations, buy with caution - 2.0 - Subpar: We do not recommend, buy with extreme caution - 1.0 - Dismal: Don't even think about buying this product Read Our Editorial Mission Statement and Testing Methodologies. The LG UltraGear evo GX9 is an obliging ultrawide gaming monitor for serious work and immersive play. It’s expertly crafted, almost like a brutalist statement piece in your office. The main downside is that, while the AI features are promising, they are not worth paying extra for in their current state. To mutilate Peter Clemenza's words from The Godfather: "Take the Tandem RGB QD-OLED panel, leave the AI upscaling." Besides, if you’re interested in buying this monitor, you probably have a GPU that's a more capable upscaler. Ultimately, the UltraGear evo GX9 is worth a look if cost is no object, but you should consider an alternative that ditches the AI features if money matters. If 39 inches is your size, the Alienware 39 5K OLED Gaming Monitor (AW3926QW) is far cheaper ($1,099 list price) and matches the UltraGear evo GX9's feature set nearly every step of the way. I’m a PCMag reviewer and ISF-certified TV calibrator focused on computer accessories, laptops, gaming monitors, and video games. I’ve been writing, playing, and complaining about games for as long as I remember, but it wasn’t until recently that I’ve been able to shout my opinions directly at a larger audience. My work has appeared on iMore, Windows Central, Android Central, and TWICE, and I have a diverse portfolio of editing work under my belt from my time spent at Scholastic and Oxford University Press. I also have a few book-author credits under my belt—I’ve contributed to the sci-fi anthology Under New Suns, and I’ve even written a Peppa Pig book.

item.title: REVIEW: Topping DX1 II review: a well-built DAC with great specification that just fails grab you by the lapels
item.description:
Source: Latest from TechRadar US in News
Its sound isn’t perfect, and it’s not without worthwhile competition, but when it comes to sonic detail and plenty of end-user options where performance is concerned, the Topping DX1 II has lots to recommend it. It looks and feels a cut above most of its price-comparable rivals, too. - +Very acceptable standard of build and finish - -Quite pronounced high-frequency roll-off Why you can trust TechRadar We spend hours testing every product or service we review, so you can be sure you're buying the best. Find out more about how we test. The world is not short of little DAC/headphone amps that want to bring a taste of authentic audio quality to your desktop experience — and here’s another one. The Topping DX1 II is a thorough update of a previous (and very competitive) in the Chinese brand's stable, and it makes a strong case for itself even before it’s started doing its thing. The aluminum casework looks and feels good and the on-paper specification is difficult to lay a glove on. It includes — deep breath — a very hi-res ESS DAC, carefully considered digital and analog architecture, USB-C for both power and data, sufficient grunt to drive most headphones without difficulty, a fistful of input and output options (including balanced analog connectivity), and the facility for plenty of end-user input where sound is concerned. The standard of construction and finish is more than adequate. And a little remote control handset takes some of the pressure off an overworked physical control interface. The difference the DX1 II can make to your audio experience when it sits between, say, your laptop and the headphones that are plugged into it is fairly profound. The Topping is by no means perfect — it doesn’t attack the top of the frequency range quite as willingly as it might, and it doesn’t have the heft to make big dynamic variations as apparent as they might be — but it’s a far more convincing and well-realized listen than your laptop alone has a hope of being. Soundstaging, rhythmic expression, detail levels and all-around musicality all enjoy a big uptick, and the way the DX1 II handles a tonal balance is one of the most uncomplicatedly enjoyable things about it. The Topping DX1 II hasn’t closed the door on other desktop-friendly headphone amp/DAC units at similar money, but it’s certainly made sure it’s on the inside of the conversation for the best on the market. Topping DX1 II review: Price & release date - Announced on May 18, 2026 (with availability from late June/July 2026) - Priced $119 / £119 (around AU$169) The Topping DX1 II is on sale now, and in the United States it costs $119. It’s £119 in the United Kingdom, while in Australia it goes for around AU$169. So, it's a little pricier than the oh-so-portable iFi Go Link Max and the bigger, hip-flask-esque iFi Uno, say, but an awful lot cheaper than the also-new iFi iDSD GR2. What exactly are you getting for your money if you go for the Topping? Read on. There’s something quite admirable about the way Topping has specified the DX1 II — I’ve used bigger and more expensive DAC/headphone amps that don’t come close to the level of this little device. It’s built around a very capable ESS ES90392QM DAC chipset and features dual-DAC architecture with a dedicated digital-to-analog converter for each channel, plus fully independent processing. Digital files of up to 32bit/384kHz and DSD256 are supported. A 16-core XMOS XU-316 assists with signal processing — just as with the dual-DAC arrangement and the fully balanced analog stage, the idea is to keep noise and distortion to an absolute minimum. Digital audio information can be delivered using either the digital optical input or the USB-C slot on the rear of the Topping. The USB-C input also provides power to the device. Outputs consist of an unbalanced 3.5mm headphone socket, a couple of balanced 4.4mm alternatives (one for headphones, the other for connecting the DX1 II to a system, a powered speaker or what-have-you) and a line-level analog output on stereo RCAs. There’s an optical output in case the digital signal needs to be preserved, and a switch to toggle between UAC 1.0 and UAC 2.0 — the first setting allows the Topping to be compatible with, say, the Nintendo Switch and the Sony PlayStation 5. Topping has made provision for an awful lot of end-user input into the way the DX1 II performs. Connect it to a computer and you can access both the ‘Home Web’ platform (from where stuff like gain can be adjusted and no fewer than eight distinct digital filters are available) and ‘Topping Tune’. This uses a simple drag-n-drop interface to allow the user to easily create and adjust PEQ settings — frequency, gain and bandwidth control across 10 bands (with independent left and right channel adjustment) can be tweaked and settings saved. It’s available across each of the DX1 II’s outputs. - Impressively detailed, easy-going sound It’s possible to make quite significant changes to the ultimate sound of the DX1 II, of course — those digital filters have a slight effect, but go crazy with the PEQ and you can achieve some pretty obvious alternations. What you can’t do, though, is defeat the things the Topping does well or fully correct its shortcomings. With a 24bit/48kHz FLAC file of The Record by Boygenius playing in the Tidal desktop app and incoming via USB-C, it doesn’t take long at all to appreciate the facility the DX1 II has with detail retrieval. It’s alert to even the most minor, most subtle occurrences in the recording, keeps an eye on the low-level dynamics of harmonic over- and undertones, and deals with transients confidently too. It gives these details good weighting, so the emphasis is always on the music and not solely on how deeply into it the Topping can peer. The tonal balance it strikes is naturalistic and pleasant, and its over-all character is, in the most positive way, easy-going and quite laid-back. It can do ‘urgency’ if it absolutely has to, of course, but its fundamental attitude is one that’s not in any way fatiguing. At no point is the Topping likely to grab you by the lapels — it’s altogether too grown-up and, again in a positive way, polite for that sort of behavior. Some of this comes about because of its relative lack of dynamic impetus. The headline dynamics of ‘quiet’ and ‘LOUD!’ in a 16bit/44.1kHz file of Life Metal by Sunn O))) are somewhat flattened by the slight shortage of headroom the DX1 II exhibits. The distance between these two positions is not as pronounced as it is when described by a DAC/headphone amp that breathes a little more deeply. Some of it is due to the Topping’s slight-but-definite tendency to roll off the highest frequencies. There’s acceptable extension into the top end, but not quite the attack or even assertiveness that makes treble sounds properly bite and shine. Elsewhere, though, the DX1 II is on firmer ground. It has a good understanding of rhythm and tempo, and controls its low-frequency activity to the point that there’s a proper sensation of fluency to the way rhythms are expressed. It can open up a soundstage to the point that even quite complex recordings get a little elbow-room, and the stage is also controlled well. And it’s worth noting that, unlike a couple of nominal rivals, the DX1 II doesn’t alter its behavior depending on the volume you’re listening at — even when playing very quietly or really quite loud, its sonic stance remains consistent. - 32 x 100 x 100mm (HxWxD) The DX1 II is usefully compact (just 32 x 100 x 100mm, HxWxD), so won’t hog space on your desktop or equipment rack. Built mostly from machined aluminum, it’s very well-made and finished — its edges are nicely rounded and it’s not remotely sharp at any of its corners. At 275g, it’s unlikely to be towed around your desktop by heavy-cabled headphones, either. Only the fact that some of the socketry is quite close together on the rear panel (which is inevitable, really) precludes the use of chunkier, more premium cables and constitutes any kind of issue. Topping DX1 II review: Usability & setup The majority of the fascia is occupied by a relatively large and gratifyingly legible LED display — volume level, selected input and what-have-you is all revealed. There’s also a relatively large turn/press dial that covers a lot of the device's functions. In all honesty, the dial is not especially intuitive when you want to do anything beyond change input or adjust volume — so it’s just as well Topping provides a little remote control handset that makes getting at your EQs, and all the rest of it, quite a lot more straightforward. Set-up is the work of a moment, of course. You’ll need to connect the USB-C slot to a source of power — maybe this is also your source of music, if it isn’t then your source will need to be connected to the optical input. Then you need to connect the DX1 II to its output device — headphones, probably, or maybe the stereo RCA outputs to an amplifier or powered speaker. And then you’re in business. - Out-and-out sound quality not up there (but you won't feel short-changed) It may only be tiny, but Topping has managed to make the DX1 II feel and, to a lesser extent, look like it deserves to cost three figures. The standard of build is well up to snuff, too — and when you take the thoroughgoing nature of its specification into account, too, the sensation of value for money is hard to argue with. The value proposition isn’t quite so cut-and-dried when it comes to out-and-out sound quality - but even here the DX1 II does more than enough right to prevent you feeling short-changed. Should I buy the Topping DX1 II? You have a desktop audio system that just consists of a laptop and some headphones Putting the DX1 II between the two will result in a significant uptick in audio quality. You want to enhance your gaming experience With UAC 1.0 selected, the signal from a console incoming and some appropriate headphones attached, gaming becomes a much more immersive experience. The Topping’s balanced output is rated at 2 x 1000mW into 32 ohms, which is more than enough to deal even quite tricky headphones. The fascia controls are not what you’d call ‘intuitive’. You enjoy the dynamic aspects of music reproduction The DX1 II is unwilling or unable to put really convincing distance between dynamic extremes . You’re especially attuned to high-frequency sound You can fiddle with the PEQ and/or the filters all you like — the Topping is inclined to roll off the top end at least a little. It’s more affordable than the DX1 II — and it looks and feels it, too — but the iFi Uno is a high-achieving little device that offers a direct, confident and information-rich sound no matter the source of music it’s connected to. I used the Topping DX1 II with an Apple MacBook Pro — connecting to the USB-C slot allowed for data transfer and power supply at the same time, and gave access to numerous music streaming services. I connected a pair of Sennheiser IE900 wired in-ear headphones to the unbalanced 3.5mm output, and also to the balanced 4.4mm output (the Sennheiser have a selection of cables with different terminations). I also connected a Sony PlayStation 5 via the optical input and sent the DX1 II output signal to the preamp in my reference system via its RCA outputs.

item.title: REVIEW: Lavazza MilkEasy Plus review: affordable frothing made easy
item.description:
Source: Latest from TechRadar US in News
The Lavazza MilkEasy Plus is an excellent-value milk frother that delivers superb performance without the hefty price tag. Delivering a versatile range of modes, great performance across both dairy and plant-based milks, and simple controls, it's a great choice for everyday use. It comes with both hot and cold foaming options, and it's easy to clean, too. Yes, a handle would make it easier to grip, and the fill markings could be clearer, but these are minor issues in an otherwise impressive package for the price. - +Great results with dairy and plant-based milk - -A little difficult to make out max fill markings - -Foamed milk takes a good while to froth - -Lacks a handle for maximum ease when pouring Why you can trust TechRadar We spend hours testing every product or service we review, so you can be sure you're buying the best. Find out more about how we test. As my millennial colleagues often say: "you don’t wanna see me before my morning coffee". And there's truth to that: having a cappuccino on first waking has become something of a ritual for me; it's more effective than an alarm clock for getting me up and doing anything useful, at least. And since getting my hands on the Lavazza MilkEasy Plus, making a quick drink every day has never been so easy. As the name suggests, the Lavazza MilkEasy Plus is an incredibly simple to use, and it’s ideal for anyone who wants to whip up a cold or hot caffeinated beverage at home. It comes with four settings: hot milk, foamed milk, hot cappuccino, and cold cappuccino. I’ve tried all of these out over a month-long period of testing, using both dairy and plant-based milks. Should you get one for yourself? Here’s my verdict. Straight off the bat, something I love about the MilkEasy Plus are its controls. A single backlit button enables you to cycle through the four different modes. Just select your preferred option, wait a few seconds, and the frothing will begin. This makes it an accessible option for anyone — no matter their level of technical or coffee know-how. Elsewhere, the included instructions are clear and concise, and after an initial clean cycle, all you have to do is plug the machine’s dock into a power outlet, place the MilkEasy Plus on top, and you’re good to go. This model comes with a magnetic whisk that easily slots inside the MilkEasy Plus — no awkward installation required. The fact that it's magnetic means that it’s also easy to remove and clean. I was able to scrub the entire device in mere seconds, and while some pesky milk residue can stick to the sides of the MilkEasy Plus, it’s really easy to get off. The whisk and lid are also dishwasher-safe, although the main chamber needs to be hand-washed. So yes, the MilkEasy Plus is a joy to use, but how does it perform? Well, I was really happy with the results every single time. With dairy milk in cappuccino mode, it whisked up a delightfully thick, creamy foam, which delivered a rich, satisfying flavor. With foamed milk, I was impressed once more, both with dairy and plant-based milks. All those plant-based baristas will be pleased to learn that this this model is "approved by Alpro", and when using oat milk, this machine really shines. The smooth, velvety texture of the foamed milk was impressive given the modest price of this model, although it did take a good three minutes to prepare. This wasn’t a big issue for me, as I set the foaming cycle in motion before drawing an espresso shot from my Lavazza A Modo Mio Smeg machine, meaning I wasn’t left waiting. But if you want the speediest performance possible, this might not be the best option for you. Not surprisingly, the hot milk and cold cappuccino modes produced similarly effective results with dairy and plant-based milk. And I was struck by how quiet the MilkEasy Plus is in use — you won't have to worry about disturbing any friends or family members if you’re making a late-night decaf coffee. While I had an overwhelmingly positive experience with the MilkEasy Plus, I do have a couple of minor quibbles that are worth a mention. Like a lot of rivals, the markings for quantity on the inside of the cup are a little difficult to read, and I found myself having to angle the machine to see the maximum fill line when adding milk. My other critique is that the MilkEasy Plus doesn't have a handle, so it can be slightly awkward to handle while pouring. This isn’t a major problem, and it’s still easy enough to grip, but a handle would have taken things up a notch. Still, this model's build quality is impressive, especially given its relatively low £79 / AU$119 (about $100) list price. The quality of the MilkEasy Plus’ results, its user-friendly controls, and easy cleaning all combine to make it a top-tier option. And while a steam wand will always be superior for latte art, this model is tough to beat for casual coffee drinkers like me. Lavazza MilkEasy Plus review: price & release date - Priced at £79 / AU$119 (about $100) The Lavazza MilkEasy Plus was released in July 2026, and is available in the UK, a number of European markets, and Australia. It isn't available directly in the US, but could conceivably be imported. This is a relatively budget-friendly model, coming in at £79 / AU$119 (about $100), making it cheaper than some of our favorite picks such as the Smeg Mini Milk Frother (£99.95, about $140 / AU$210) and the Dreo Baristamaker ($99 / £119.99, about AU$150). Should I buy the Lavazza MilkEasy Plus? The Lavazza MilkEasy Plus has both hot and cold foaming capabilities, and produces great results across the board. Just press the backlit button, select your preferred type, and your milk will be ready in minutes. You want a simple and easy-to-clean machine The Lavazza MilkEasy Plus is very easy to clean. The transparent lid and whisk can be placed in the dishwasher, and the main chamber can be hand-washed in a matter of seconds. The dock can’t be submerged in water, though, so wipe it clean with a wet or dry cloth instead. The MilkEasy Plus produces thick, creamy results, but it perhaps lacks the close-control that a steam-wand provides for doing latte art. You want the speediest performance around While the MilkEasy Plus is a smooth, quiet operator, it’s not the speediest performer around. It took a good few minutes for a foamed milk cycle to finish. For more instant results, you may want to look elsewhere. Lavazza MilkEasy Plus review: also consider This machine shares a lot of similarities with the MilkEasy Plus. It's simple to use, produces thick hot or cold foam that would work well for regular or iced cappuccinos, and it can be cleaned in a matter of seconds. Its compact and sleek design also helps it to stand out from a lot of the competition. Read our full Smeg Mini Milk Frother review. While the Dreo Baristamaker is on the bulky side, we were really impressed by its consistent results, quiet operation, and ease of use. If you want a higher maximum milk capacity, this is a great alternative to the MilkEasy Plus. Read our full Dreo Baristamaker review. I spent one month testing the Lavazza MilkEasy Plus, using it as a key part of my coffee-making setup almost every day. I tried all four of the frothing modes, and made sure to use whole and semi-skimmed milk, as well as oat milk to assess consistency across different types. I used the Lavazza MilkEasy Plus alongside my Lavazza A Modo Mio Smeg capsule coffee machine for this review. More generally, I’ve spent years testing gadgets here at TechRadar, where I serve as a Senior Reviews Writer. I’ve tested everything from home products such as the Dreo Smart Misting Fan 516S to Dolby Atmos soundbars, like the Marshall Heston 120.

item.title: REVIEW: IQUNIX MQ80 low profile mechanical keyboard review
item.description:
Source: Latest from Tom's Hardware
The IQUNIX MQ80 is well-made and super stylish, but it’s not quite the instant sell it used to be. Catch this one if you don’t like magnetic switches, but otherwise wait for a sale. - +Aluminum construction and PBT keycaps make it incredibly durable - +Gasket mounted for soft keystrokes and enhanced acoustics - +Excellent sound, feel, and responsiveness - -Switches aren’t adjustable, limited options available Why you can trust Tom's Hardware Our expert reviewers spend hours testing and comparing products and services so you can choose the best for you. Find out more about how we test. When it comes to mechanical keyboards, IQUNIX has always been ahead of the curve. Before COVID turned the mainstream onto mechanical keyboards, the company had already been releasing some of the best mechanical keyboards available, quietly making the case for PBT keycaps and premium materials that have since become the norm. With a catalog of traditional mechanical keyboards under its belt, it’s not surprising that the company would be ready to branch into new territory. It has the Hall Effect demographic covered with its EZ series, but the MQ80 goes another direction entirely. It takes all of the lessons the company learned about how to create an exceptional typing and gaming experience and compressed it. It’s all aluminum, low profile, and offers some of the best-sounding keystrokes of its kind, but steep competition and poor portability hold it back from being the go-to pick it might otherwise be. Design and Construction of the IQUNIX MQ80 The IQUNIX MQ80 breaks the mold for IQUNIX, but carries the same 75-percent layout as countless mechanical keyboards before it. The form factor is sometimes referred to as a “Compact TKL,” since it shares most of the same keys — minus the blank spaces in between. The result is a condensed slab of keys, including a full function row, arrow cluster, and seven navigation and editing keys. Nothing too out of the ordinary there, but the MQ80 marries that compact layout with an impressively low height of only 0.4 inches (10.8mm) at the front and 1.08 inches (27.5mm) in the rear. The keycaps are the same height across every row, and while they're scooped to keep your finger centered above the switch, they otherwise feel identical below the finger tip. This makes it an easy transition if you’re coming from a laptop or Apple Magic Keyboard, but first-time LP users should be prepared for a learning curve. The keyboard is wireless and supports both 2.4GHz and Bluetooth 5.1 connections, as well as wired if you need to use it while it’s recharging. It sports a 4,000 mAh battery which IQUNIX claims can sustain the keyboard for up to 350 hours. This is with the usual caveats of that being over Bluetooth with all of the lighting disabled, etc. etc. — but I was able to use it for close to two weeks between recharges, even with the lighting on. The MQ80 is a bit of a curiosity, if I’m being honest. It's thin, yes, but it’s certainly not light. It uses a heavy, CNC-milled aluminum case, just like the company’s prior models and countless others aiming for that “premium feel.” It’s a case study in how looks can be deceiving. In fact, it has been a pretty common occurrence for people to comment on how surprising its weight is. The keyboard tips the scales at 2.6 pounds, which is around what you encounter with a full-size mechanical keyboard or nicer TKL. From a low profile keyboard that everyone assumes will be airy and effortless to carry around, it flies in the face of what you might expect. So while technically, yes, it’s a portable keyboard (IQUNIX even provides a nice hardshell carrying case to tote it around in), it's not one I could see most people wanting to carry every day. Instead, this seems designed to live on your desk, providing a solid option for fans of the profile who prefer to use it for all of their typing — not just on the go. In typical IQUNIX fashion, the MQ80 is built to an enthusiast's standard. The case features intricate milling with plenty of small accents that lend it a vaguely cyberpunk impression. The keycaps feature colored legends and contrasting accents that complete its visual identity. The keyboard is available in white or black with keycaps to match, and both look fetching. The keycaps are made of thick PBT plastic. They have a light texture to add some grip to your typing experience and use dye sublimated legends that won't chip or fade over time. The switches below those keycaps are Kailh Rose Red, a lightweight linear switch with a 40g actuation force, 2.8mm of travel distance, and a 1.2mm actuation point. Despite their shortness, they offer 70% of the movement of a full-height switch. This makes them easier to transition to in how they feel to bottom out, but they still feel sensitive. This is a keyboard to use with a light touch or you'll find yourself with strings of single letters or running from cover before you mean to. The switches are hot-swappable with any Kailh Choc V2 alternative, but there just aren't many options. Gateron has run away with the variety end of the low profile switch market, but you can swap them out if you're inclined to do so. The keyboard features per-key RGB backlighting, customizable within the VIA web configurator or with shortcut keys. The keycaps aren't backlit, however, so it's not great for use in the dark if you aren't a touch typist. The internal structure of the keyboard is where things get really interesting. The MQ80 came into the world following a run of pre-built custom keyboards IQUNIX produced under its SUPER product line. It pulled direct influence from the boutique, limited run, group buy custom keyboards popular on r/mechanicalkeyboards. All of those lessons come into play with the MQ80. Beneath the keys lies a multi-layer assembly that makes even the best gaming keyboards look simple in comparison. It's an intentional system meant to filter and refine the sound and feel of every keystroke without the need to customize or adjust anything yourself. Moving from the top down, the switches snap into a fiberglass (FR4) plate, a middle-ground material that balances firmness with crisp keystrokes. Beneath the plate and PCB are two layers of foam, each with different acoustic properties, and a plastic film. The first layer of foam is thick PORON and fills in the empty space between the switches, plate, and PCB. It cuts reverb and helps isolate each switch. A much thinner, less dense sheet of IXPE foam and a plastic PET sheet sit below the switches to add a crispness and pop to each keystroke. Below the circuit board is another layer of PORON foam that filters soundwaves that pass through and cushion each press. Finally, in the very bottom of the case is another layer of IXPE foam intended to reflect mid-range sounds and act as a final buffer before hitting the aluminum of the case. It sounds like a lot and it is, but it doesn't end there. The PCB assembly attaches to the case with a modified gasket mount ("Le-Tray Gasket Mount") that imparts some of the qualities of gasket mounting into this much slimmer design. Six arms from the assembly attach to the case with silicone buffers, holding it aloft to deliver pillowy bottom outs. As a wireless keyboard, IQUNIX also had to fit a battery into its slim frame. It's surprisingly large given the space constraints with a 4,000mAh capacity. This translates into 350 hours of rated uptime, but only when using Bluetooth and no RGB backlighting. In practice, keeping RGB on high and using 2.4GHz, it lasts around 45 hours but your specific figure will depend on use. While there's an obvious pre-requisite to prefer low profile keys, you'll also need to be a fan of linear switches. And not just that, you'll need to be a fan of lightweight, fast actuating low profile switches with keycaps that feel identical under your fingers. If I sound a little salty, I'm not. It's just that I've used hundreds of mechanical keyboards and typed A Song of Ice and Fire worth of words on them, including more than a fair share of competing low profile keyboards, and it's still a pain in the ass to switch back to them. At least at first, because you do get used to it and the light touch required. Before long, I remembered to pay special attention to the navigation bumps on the "F" and "J" keys. Once everything clicked, I honestly felt faster and more nimble as a typist. Surprisingly, this didn't translate into actual WPM in my case. I average right around 110 WPM on my day-to-day full height keyboard. Swapping to the MQ80, my raw speed increased slightly, likely due to the lightweight switches and the floating posture I adopted to accommodate its height. My actual average words-per-minute on MonkeyType actually decreased to 105 WPM due to having to backspace to correct typos. So, typing speed is a bit of a wash (at least for me) but it's hard to argue that the sound and feel of typing on the keyboard is less than exceptional. The multiple layers of sound dampening quiet and deepen the sound of each keystroke in a satisfying way. The Le-Tray Gasket Mount system also gives bottom outs a softness that's reminiscent of, but slightly stiffer than, the gasket mounts used on most full height gaming keyboards. The thing is, since IQUNIX launched the MQ80 to Kickstarter in early 2025, Nuphy released the third iteration of its Air75 series, the Air75 V3, and it delivers a typing experience that I feel is at least as good and is objectively more customizable with its Gateron low profile switches and tactile and silent switch options at checkout. As a heavy handed typist, I prefer a lot of tactility, especially on a keyboard with perfectly flat rows. The only option for "not a light tactile" were Kailh Black Cloud switches and would have run me half the cost of the keyboard itself. None of this is to say that the typing experience is bad. It's genuinely not. IQUNIX knows its stuff. All of this is simply to say that there's an important trade-off and if you don't like light linear switches or paying a premium to replace them, the MQ80 probably isn't the keyboard for you. If you like that light touch, the custom keyboard-esque feel of its keystrokes filtering through all of that foam and milled aluminum, then you're probably going to love it. Most of the same considerations from the typing experience apply to gaming as well, but fragging enemies is really where the MQ80 felt most at home to me. Those lightweight switches that were a liability to typing accuracy suddenly feel like hair triggers. If you're connected using the 2.4 GHz dongle or plugged in via USB, its 1,000 Hz polling rate ensures that every keystroke comes through instantly - though, it still doesn't compare to the growing number of 8,000 Hz keyboards out there on paper. Whether you'll be able to tell the difference is up for debate. While the layers of cushioning and damping don't have a direct impact on how effective the MQ80 is for gaming, much like typing, they just make the experience that much more pleasant. Apart from its switches, there's a dearth of dedicated gaming features unique to the keyboard. The keys are reprogrammable and support string macros, but you won't find a fancy software suite to support the experience here. Instead, IQUNIX went open source and the MQ80 is better for it. Where the MQ80 comes into its own is its programmability. Unlike many traditional gaming keyboards, it doesn't have downloadable software that needs to stay running in the background. Instead, IQUNIX opted to support VIA, a web-based configurator that allows you to make changes on the fly while also saving them to the keyboard. It's simple on the surface, but is surprisingly powerful once you dive into it. Every key can carry up to four different actions or macros, broken into layers for quick shortcut access. Much like holding Shift, you hold or tap a key of your choice and access those additional layers of keymaps. While this functionality isn't unique to VIA or the MQ80 by any means, big gaming companies usually require you to keep their software running to access layered functions (ex. Razer HyperShift). Here, every change is written directly to the keyboard's firmware and will work on any machine, exactly as programmed. The web client itself is fairly simple. You have a graphic of your keyboard layout with all of your current mappings on display. Underneath are all of the different commands that can be mapped, including things like media controls, additional F-keys (all the way to F24), macros, RGB controls, and virtually anything else you might want to assign to a keystroke. The biggest feature you'll miss out on, apart from proprietary features like game-synced RGB backlighting, is the ability to assign backlight colors to individual keys. It's possible to change the brightness, hue, and saturation across its dozen or so preset animations, but creating an entirely custom lighting scheme requires creating your own code and flashing it to the keyboard manually. The IQUNIX MQ80 is a very good keyboard. For a lot of users, I'm confident that they would describe it as "Great" or even "Amazing." I wouldn't fault them for that. This is essentially the luxury option in the low profile space at this point. But it's too heavy to easily tote around without questioning your life choices. If portability is important to you, I highly recommend the Nuphy Air75 V3. Or, if you're looking for something a little more office friendly than the Nuphy, the Lofree Flow 2 is another great choice that also comes with a tactile switch option. At the end of the day, all three of these options are good for the money but only the MQ80 feels like a luxury option thanks to its heavy case. If you're not planning on carrying it back and forth to work and you like a fast switch, the MQ80 is a solid choice.

item.title: REVIEW: Movavi Video Editor 27 review
item.description:
Source: Latest from TechRadar US in News
Movavi had already released a competent and affordable video editor, and they’ve built upon this sound foundation with their new ‘Templates’ feature which is much more versatile and customisable than it appears at first glance. A great addition to quickly introduce a bit of style and panache to your project. Why you can trust TechRadar We spend hours testing every product or service we review, so you can be sure you're buying the best. Find out more about how we test. When I last looked at Movavi Video Editor, I was quite impressed by its capabilities - it's one of the best video editing software for beginners in my experience. But time waits for no computer program, and as version 27 has recently been released, I thought it was time to check how it has improved. - Perpetual license is way more expensive for Americans You can grab Movavi Video Editor 27 from the official site by clicking here. Let’s face it: everything’s getting more expensive. Whether it’s food, petrol, or subscriptions, the price keeps going ever higher, so it was with trepidation that I looked at Movavi’s current pricing structure. However, it’s not all doom and gloom: Movavi have actually lowered their prices. Should you decide to pay monthly for your video editor, you’ll need to fork out $20, €19 or £18, but the big incentive is to pay yearly, as it’s only $55, €44, or £41, which is a little over 2 months’ worth. It’s not as cheap as free of course (like DaVinci Resolve), but it’s a heck of a lot cheaper than Adobe Premiere Pro (which would set you back $276 each year). If you’d rather pay once and actually own the software you’re downloading, a perpetual licence is also available for £150, €90 or £90 (the massive discrepancy between currencies is… puzzling). And perhaps best of all, the software is multi-platform, allowing you to work with it, whether you use a PC or a Mac. If you’re not sure about investing in this application, there’s a free trial you can access. A watermark will be added to any output, and your projects are limited to 60 seconds in length. Still, it should be enough to give you an idea of what you can do with Movavi Video Editor. - The software still doesn’t know which language your OS is set to Last time I checked out Movavi, back when it was on version 25, I made a point of stating that unusually, the first time you launch the software, you’re not greeted with an interface in your own native tongue, or at the very least in English. Instead, all the menus are in Japanese. That’s not an issue if you know that language, but if you’re more familiar with those that use the Latin alphabet, you’re faced with an unexpected challenge. Thankfully, if you grab a screenshot of the interface and submit it to Google Translate, the solution will become more obvious, and changing the default language then becomes a trivial matter. But it’s disappointing to see that after all this time, Movavi still treats this as a feature, not a bug. Software should be able to detect the OS’s chosen language and default to that when you launch it. I’m surprised Movavi still insists on making life difficult for many of its customers. - Excellent video editor with a wealth of useful, powerful, and well implemented tools - Shame so many of them are locked behind subscription plans Initial frustrations aside, when it comes to video editing - what the software is designed for - Movavi Video Editor does a sterling job. It starts with mousing over an imported clip in the media section. Doing that allows you to preview the clip as you move the cursor over it, enabling you to set in and out points with ease. You can work with multiple layers of course, although there is a base layer beneath which you can’t add other clips, which can be a little annoying if you like to create complex projects and move clips around a lot. There are Titles, Transitions, Effects, and Elements aplenty, all organised by category with a handy search field available, although many of those are restricted behind a paywall. These are identified by a little ‘crown’ logo, top right of their thumbnails. You can still use them in your project, but you’ll be informed upon export that you need to purchase a subscription to be able to share any video with them in it, for either €36 a month, or €110 a year, which, I’m sure you can tell, is much more expensive than the actual program itself. This can be annoying but it’s entirely possible to restrict yourself to non-premium assets by setting the filter for each section to ‘free’. The Tools section houses important features, such as image stabilisation, background removal, green green work, and an AI-based subtitle feature which worked incredibly well when I tried it out. Thankfully, everything stored in that section is part of the software’s base cost. But all of this was already part of Movavi Video Editor. The big innovation that’s being introduced in version 27, is Templates. - Templates offers a great and versatile way to spice up your project - Can be used wholesale or just choosing just the parts you’re interested in The concept of Templates is pretty clever: editing can be hard and time consuming, and if you just want to put something out there but lack the skills or experience, it can really be a chore. So Movavi have created a large collection of ready-made templates which you can add to your project. One template could be your entire video, or alternatively, be part of a larger one. It’s also entirely possible to add multiple templates to the same project. These are organised into 12 categories, from Beauty and Fashion, to Gaming, to Marketing and Promo, and more. And it probably won’t surprise you to know that nearly all these templates include some premium features of some kind, although each category has at least one free option for you to choose. Dragging a template to a project expands it into various sections, each of which lets you know how many placeholders within it need to be replaced. Some sections don’t give you the option to replace theirs which is odd, but it’s a simple matter of deleting them entirely and adding one of your own clips in their place. As for actually replacing those placeholders, it wasn’t as intuitive as I had expected, but once you’re aware of the concept, the process is quite simple: click on the ‘clips to replace’ text on the section’s representation in your timeline, to reveal the placeholder’s large thumbnail above it. Clicking on that thumbnail opens a window containing all the media you imported into this project. Select the one you want, choose the part of it you’d like to use, and click on ‘Apply’. Repeat that for every placeholder. Need more customisation? Double-click on a Template’s Section to reveal its ‘Clip Settings’. In addition to offering you another way to replace those placeholder clips, you also have other options, such as customising the text fields, or checking the applied effects, for instance. These templates also come with a soundtrack which you’re free to use or discard, just like you can reorder or delete the sections it came with, which actually allows you to mix and match parts of different templates to create your own unique project in minutes rather than hours. I found it a great fun way to quickly build something original. Should I buy Movavi Video Editor 27? Buy it if... You’re into video editing and are looking for an affordable application that will let you do just that, and you appreciate the addition of versatile and customisable templates to speed up your work. Don't buy it if... You don’t spend enough time editing video to warrant paying for such software, so you’d rather find something that’s free, even if it means having fewer tools at your disposal. Movavi Video Editor is multi-platform, being compatible with Windows and Macs alike, which is a great thing (sorry Linux users). I always like to test such software primarily with the underdog (or I prefer just Macs… you decide). In this instance, I put it through its paces on a recent laptop sporting Apple Silicon, as based on my previous exploration of this software when it was at version 25, I had concluded it needed a ‘decently powerful machine’ to run effectively. The software ran incredibly smoothly and was very responsive. I particularly liked the way it looks but, to be honest, that could be due to the fact the interface, and even the way the clips are presented in the timeline, resembles Final Cut Pro, one of my preferred video editing platforms. For more creative apps, we've tested and reviewed the best video editing software, the best free video editing software, and the best video editing apps for mobile devices.

item.title: SALES: The hottest AI wearables and gadgets you should know about
item.description:
Source: TechCrunch
A slew of AI-powered gadgets on the market aims to integrate artificial intelligence into our daily lives like never before. Some of these AI wearables — including necklaces, rings, and wristbands, as well as portable devices — serve as productivity tools, while others claim to act as friendly companions listening to your everyday thoughts. Even OpenAI is working on a compact AI companion device. Below, we’ve rounded up some of the most notable devices. Bee is an affordable pendant priced at $49.99 that can either be clipped to your clothing or worn like a fitness band. This device records everything it hears and learns your routines and preferences to create reminders and notes for you. It even features a mute button for those times you want some privacy. The companion app (currently available only on iOS) is included with a $19 monthly subscription. The app allows you to interact with Bee directly and ask it questions. You can also get key takeaways from your day and chronological transcripts of your conversations. Amazon acquired the wearables startup in July 2025, launching its first new products earlier this month. Amazon introduced two new devices: the Bee Frontier, priced at $74.99, which can be worn on the wrist or clipped to clothing, and the Bee Eclipse, priced at $99.99, a credit-card-sized device that attaches magnetically to the back of a smartphone. Both offer the same core functionality as the previous generation, positioning Bee as a more affordable alternative to AI devices such as the Plaud Note and Plaud NotePin. Users can also choose to connect Bee to Alexa. Friend is one of the most hyped entrants in the “personal AI” device market. This $129 white pendant hangs around your neck and functions as an emotional support companion. It recognizes your tone and mood, allowing you to chat with it as if it were a friend. It connects to your phone via Bluetooth and constantly listens, ready to respond or send you proactive messages, like wishing you good luck before an interview. However, it has also faced criticism, including backlash against its subway ad campaign in NYC. People vandalized the ads, writing messages like “surveillance capitalism.” Likely as an attempt to stay relevant, the company recently unveiled a major product update, introducing a new voice feature. Under the name “Friend 2.0,” the updated device includes a built-in speaker that allows it to communicate with users and express a more distinctive personality. Formerly known as Rewind, Limitless is another conversation-recording pendant priced at $99. This device continuously listens, transcribing meetings, calls, and conversations (with consent) into searchable and summarized knowledge. It’s ideal for professionals, especially journalists, looking to recall important discussions. The device is designed to be phone-adjacent, allowing you to perform tasks such as booking flights, ordering meals, and controlling apps without needing to pull out your phone each time. Following a crucial software update that rectified previous performance issues, the Rabbit R1 now boasts expanded AI features. item.title: SALES: Six of the Greatest Movie Soundtracks From This Century
item.description:
Source: The Atlantic
This is an edition of The Atlantic Daily, a newsletter that guides you through the biggest stories of the day, helps you discover new ideas, and recommends the best in culture. Sign up for it here. A great movie soundtrack can be just as memorable as the film itself. A few notes might bring an entire scene rushing back, and an old song can find new life in the right movie. Below, six Atlantic staffers share their favorite film soundtracks of the 21st century. One Battle After Another (streaming on HBO Max and Prime Video) Beneath its cat-and-mouse tale about fascism and rebellion, Paul Thomas Anderson’s 2025 Best Picture Oscar winner is a masterpiece of cadence. The story progresses in slow creeps and sudden, skittering leaps. Characters crash together and pull apart like excited molecules. The sizzling energy owes to an unusual process: Anderson hired the Radiohead multi-instrumentalist Jonny Greenwood to compose music before shooting began and then edited Greenwood’s work. The soundtrack pairs percussive piano with drums hooked to robotic circuits to create backbeats as insistent and unsteady as hiccups. Twanging guitars and symphonic strings express unsettled, ugly-pretty chords. The effect is an astonishingly original reminder that social movements are but collections of individuals, each squiggling along their own trajectory. Darkest Hour (streaming on Apple TV and Prime Video) I love soundtracks, but my favorites—Glory, Miller’s Crossing, Crimson Tide—are all at least 30 years old. I am a sucker for a John Williams march or an elegiac Thomas Newman moment, but when I consulted my playlist, I found that one soundtrack kept rising to the top: Darkest Hour, by Dario Marianelli (with piano by Víkingur Ólafsson). The movie follows Winston Churchill’s first days in office, in 1940, after France fell and Britain stood alone against the Nazis. The score alternates between piano meditations and orchestral flight; like Churchill, it is fussy and elegant, quiet and then bombastic. It conveys the tension and urgency in the man and the moment. The final track, “We Shall Fight,” plays over Churchill’s speech to Parliament in which he vows to never surrender to evil. It is a moving and uplifting piece, but also tragic: He knew the horrors that awaited, and he led Britain to its fate anyway. The Lord of the Rings: The Fellowship of the Ring (streaming on HBO Max) On the subject of movie music, much comes to mind. My single favorite piece of original movie music this century might be “The Alien,” Ben Salisbury and Geoff Barrow’s eerie composition for Annihilation; my favorite repurposed song might be Plumtree’s “Scott Pilgrim,” the lovey-dovey indie-rock namesake of Scott Pilgrim vs. the World. Jon Brion’s off-kilter bricolage for Punch-Drunk Love, the torch ballads of A Star Is Born, the uncut Daft Punk–ness of Tron: Legacy—all of this matters to me. However, play two seconds of “Concerning Hobbits,” and I’m back in the Shire, awaiting the appearance of a great wizard and hanging out with my vertically challenged friends. Howard Shore’s score for Fellowship, and for the rest of the Lord of the Rings series, is both transportive and formfitting, making Peter Jackson’s movie sound as epic as it looks. Shrek 2 (streaming on Peacock) When I first watched Shrek 2, I was far more interested in the movie’s ridiculous fairy-tale antics than in the music. Years later, I’ve come to appreciate that the soundtrack is every bit as good as the movie itself. The song choices, including Counting Crows’ “Accidentally in Love” in the opening sequence, are absurdly perfect for a film about a green ogre meeting his in-laws. The soundtrack also features David Bowie, Nick Cave, and Tom Waits, but the undisputed highlight is Jennifer Saunders’s rendition of “Holding Out for a Hero” as the Fairy Godmother, which turns the climactic rescue scene into a musical spectacle that has no right to be as thrilling as it is. A villain belting out a Bonnie Tyler song while a giant gingerbread man storms a castle? As a kid, I thought it was the height of cinema. I may have outgrown some of my other childhood favorites, but I still think the Fairy Godmother deserves a Grammy. Challengers (streaming on Paramount+ and Apple TV) Ever need to outrun a serial killer, punch a bully, or fight a bear? Have I got the soundtrack for you! Nothing gets me going quite like Trent Reznor and Atticus Ross’s magnus opus, the soundtrack for Luca Guadagnino’s film Challengers. (To fans of their work for The Social Network—sorry, this one’s simply better!) The film makes the compelling argument that everything in life is about sex, except sex, which is about tennis. The pulsing, almost panic-inducing score draws on Berlin techno and ’90s rave music to heighten the anxiety of the film’s central love triangle. The frenzied sounds amplify the adrenaline that elite tennis players feel as they play (and sometimes kiss) each other. Listening to the climactic track, “Match Point,” one almost feels like the tennis ball being flung around the court. Whenever I need to crush a deadline or motivate myself to tackle a hard task, the Challengers soundtrack is my go-to. Plus, I once heard it played in a nightclub, and I haven’t been the same since. Sicario (streaming on HBO Max and Hulu) The Icelandic composer Jóhann Jóhannsson’s work in Sicario has been ripped off a million times. The beautifully foreboding noises he pioneered and perfected for Denis Villeneuve’s ultra-stylish, very violent feds-versus-cartels thriller—the subterranean bass groans, the trapped-in-the-birth-canal percussion, the tinnitus-like swarms of strings—are now part of the standard kit of horror-movie soundtracking: You can hear them, in degraded form, everywhere. But Jóhannsson, unlike his imitators, had other registers, other capacities: Sicario also features the elegiac “Desert Music,” which sounds less like the industrial metal nihilists Godflesh and more like, I don’t know, Bach. Something else Jóhannsson shared with Bach? I think he was probably a genius. Here are three Sunday reads from The Atlantic: - The Only Living Pickpocket in New York, a crime thriller about an aging pickpocket who steals a valuable USB drive and becomes the target of a vengeful crime family (in theaters Friday) - Nocturne, a crime-drama series about a Pennsylvania detective who enlists his FBI-agent protégé to catch a serial killer (streaming Friday on Apple TV) - The Brightness, a novel by Chad Harbach about two young women who navigate friendship, love, and ambition as they face life-changing decisions in their 20s (out Tuesday) Centuries before bookstores had shelves labeled romance and fictional hockey players locked eyes across the ice, the love story, with all of its attendant joys and sorrows, was an organizing principle of life—and of literature. The sentiment that another person might “complete” us enchanted both Plato and Jerry Maguire, and the search for that someone, along with the desire to understand why it can hurt so bad, has animated fiction from the beginning. The list below is an effort to name those love stories: novels, of course, but also poetry, plays, and short stories—that we consider to be the most enduring. We asked a jury of scholars, librarians, critics, and authors across genres, as well as many colleagues, to name their favorite titles that were originally written in English. We thought of our own personal touchstones, deliberated over the choices, and emerged with a group of standouts: 50 titles you won’t soon forget. Explore a collection of some of the highest-scoring images from the 2026 Epson International Pano Awards.

item.title: SALES: Where to Stay When Visiting Alaska's Denali National Park
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler
With broad river valleys, colorful meadows peppered with fireweed and lupine, forests thick with spruce and aspen, and the snow-covered Alaska Range rising in the distance, Denali National Park and Preserve is one of those places that can still feel startlingly wild no matter how many times you visit. At 6.1 million acres, it’s larger than Massachusetts, and the sheer scale of the national park means a trip here can look very different depending on where you choose to stay. I lived in Alaska full-time for eight years (and now split my time between Alaska and Colorado) and have been to Denali often. Over time, I got to know the best places travelers can base themselves in and around the park. The challenge of planning a trip to Denali isn’t necessarily finding somewhere to stay, but figuring out which part of the vast region makes the most sense as a home base for what you want to see. The cluster of lodges just outside the entrance, where restaurants, outfitters, and bus departures are all close at hand, is one of the go-to spots for first-time visitors. Nearby Healy and the long stretches of the Parks Highway offer more breathing room, with cabins, vacation rentals, and quieter stays scattered north and south of the park. And for travelers who want to go much deeper, Kantishna sits nearly 90 miles down Denali Park Road, offering a handful of remote lodges and the rare chance to stay deep inside the national park itself. I’ve selected the best stays across that spectrum, from full-service hotels and family-friendly cabins to secluded backcountry lodges and even a chalet set on a glacier just miles from the summit of North America’s highest peak. Read on for my favorite places to stay near Denali National Park in Alaska. How to plan a trip to Denali National Park and Preserve How do you get to Denali National Park? There is just one major highway leading to Denali National Park: George Parks Highway, which connects Denali to Fairbanks, about two and a half hours to the north, and Anchorage, about four and a half hours to the south. Both cities have well-connected airports and multiple car rental options. You don't need a car to get around in Denali National Park, but if you visit during the shoulder season, you can drive your own vehicle as far into the park as road conditions allow. If you don't want to drive, limited motor coach services can get you to Denali during the summer. The most luxurious option for reaching Denali is the Alaska Railroad, which, like the George Parks Highway, runs from Anchorage to Fairbanks and vice versa. The train runs directly through Denali's entrance and drops visitors off just a five-minute walk from the park's visitor center. When is the best time to visit Denali National Park? Denali National Park's peak season is mid-May through mid-September. Most tour, lodging, and restaurant amenities shut down as soon as the peak season ends, but if you're prepared to DIY a trip in winter conditions—or want to book a day tour out of Fairbanks—you can still visit during the winter. Visiting during the early-May or mid- to late-September shoulder seasons offers a more secluded experience. Amenities and tour options are extremely limited, but September in particular is a beautiful time for exploring the park when the weather cooperates. What are the best things to do in Denali National Park? Perhaps the best-known excursion in Denali is taking a bus ride on the lone road running into the park. Narrated tour buses and hop-on, hop-off transit buses used to run all the way down the 92-mile park road—but an ongoing land slump has forced partial closure of the road, so all vehicle traffic currently turns around at mile 43. For a quick (and free) taste of the park road, you can catch the courtesy shuttle that runs between the Denali Visitor Center and Savage River (mile 15 of the park road). You can also rent a bicycle from Bike Denali, about a (bikeable) mile outside the park entrance, and explore as far as you'd like along the park road, or drive your personal vehicle as far as mile 15 during peak season, although the small parking area at Savage River fills up fast. It's natural to expect a glimpse of North America's tallest mountain, Denali, when you come to the park that bears its name. But you'll have to venture to at least mile 9 of the park road before the elevation is high enough to reveal 20,310' Denali. If you're feeling adventurous, you can also hike to the top of the aptly named Mountain Vista trail, at about mile 12, for more views. The mountain is often obscured by clouds, so if you don't get to see it while in the park, don't despair: You can also catch a glimpse from the Alaska Railroad trains or, if you're driving, from several well-marked waysides along the Parks Highway. Denali is home to a handful of beautiful hiking trails, including the beloved Savage River and Savage Alpine trails, as well as the stunning Triple Lakes Trail, where you might be able to add beavers to your wildlife-viewing checklist. You're also welcome to hike off-trail from the park road—just hop off at any likely-looking pullout and explore. No matter where you hike, it's important that you carry bear spray—which you can rent from the Alaska Geographic store in the park, next to the Denali Visitor Center—and know what to do if you encounter wildlife. Park rangers are also available to help you choose a hiking destination and coach you on how to handle wildlife encounters. They also lead a variety of group activities, including hikes both on- and off-trail. Denali National Park is home to the National Park Service's only working kennel of sled dogs. Rangers demonstrate how they work with the dogs two to three times per day throughout the summer; you can walk to the kennels from the park entrance, or catch a free shuttle bus. You'll see a wide variety of other tour options advertised for Denali National Park, including whitewater rafting, horseback riding, ATV tours, and jeep tours. With very few exceptions, these take place along the boundary of the park, not actually in it. But adventuring alongside Denali can be a fine—and thrilling—way to spend your visit. Among companies operating just outside the park, Denali Horseback Tours is a perennial favorite. Their reliable steeds take you off into the hills for beautiful vistas overlooking the park and neighboring lands, without any of the noise or exhaust from a jeep or ATV tour. If you do want the thrill of a motor-driven vehicle, though, Denali ATV Adventures is hugely popular. A last (and favorite) way of seeing Denali at near-distance is from the water. Whitewater rafting tours from companies like the family-owned Denali Raft Adventures take you down the Nenana River, which forms the natural boundary on the east side of Denali National Park. Rafting excursions range from pulse-pounding to relatively sedate, so there’s something for almost everybody. If you’re ready to splurge on a once-in-a-lifetime experience, Alaska Alpine Adventures is an excellent guide service that does have the required permits to work inside the park. Just note that their custom hiking and backpacking tours demand a fairly high level of physical fitness. What area should you stay in near Denali National Park? Denali National Park is notably absent of a traditional gateway town, a characteristic that sets it apart from many other national parks. The National Park Service's focus on preserving the park's natural state has led to policies that limit large-scale development and urbanization. The best areas to stay in therefore include spots directly on the mountain; in Kantishna, a bustling gold mining hub situated 90 miles into the park; and a smattering of hotels, resorts, and Airbnbs between Healy (about 11 miles north of the park entrance) and Cantwell (approximately 30 miles south of the park entrance). You can also choose to stay in Talkeetna, about a two-and-a-half-hour drive from the entrance, roughly halfway between Anchorage and Denali. Keep in mind that if you plan to head to Kantishna, with the closure of the Denali Park Road beyond mile 43 until at least summer 2027 due to the Pretty Rocks Landslide, the only way to get there is currently by bush plane or helicopter, providing guests with rare, near-exclusive access to the park’s wild interior. “The Canyon” (otherwise known as “Glitter Gulch,” the hub for tourism just outside the park, with various services, tour companies, shops, and restaurants catering to visitors), is an area that exists almost exclusively for tourism—locals don’t live there.
