item.title: SALES: 19 best places to visit in January 2027: for warm weather, icy mountains or buzzy city breaks
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK
I will die on this hill: January is the most depressing month of the year when you live in Europe or on the East Coast of the United States – which makes it the perfect time to organise a lovely trip. And the good news is, you're spoilt for choice when it comes to the best places to visit in January. All the fun and good food of the Christmas festivities are now a distant memory, summer is still incredibly far away, and if we add the terrible weather and everyone trying to ‘be healthy’ after the excesses of December, the only way to get some joy in January is to hop on a plane – whether that’s a long-haul flight to a sunny Caribbean island or a short flight to the Alps to enjoy both the skiing and the après-ski. Personally, I like a bit of both. During particularly harsh winters, I always long to be in Latin America, having breakfast with plenty of pão de queijo and a fresh açaí bowl in Brazil, or eating tacos and drinking micheladas in Mexico. When autumn has been particularly mild, as it has this year, I'm partial to a week of skiing – mainly hitting the spa and happily participating in raclette parties, if I'm being honest – in the French Alps. The possibilities are endless and, interestingly, January is actually one of the best months to explore some of the world's most beautiful destinations, whether you're after winter sunshine or snow-covered mountains. In Southeast Asia and across the Caribbean, sunny skies, warm temperatures and idyllic beaches make for the perfect escape from the European winter. Closer to home, lean into the winter weather in Europe's snow-clad landscapes, whizzing on skis across the Dolomites or chasing the northern lights in Iceland. To really start the year off right, consider jetting off to one of these destinations in the last few days of December, just in time to see world-famous firework displays on New Year's Eve in Dubai, for example. Without further ado, here are the best holiday destinations to head to in January 2027.

item.title: SALES: I’ve Lived In The Alps For Six Seasons. These Are The European Resorts Actually Worth Your Time—and Money.
item.description:
Source: Outside Magazine
More Americans are traveling to the Alps than ever before. At the same time, the conditions surrounding travel plans are changing rapidly. Snow coverage is dwindling, the dollar is losing value, and more U.S. based megapasses are Americans are using their megapasses overseas. Having spent several winters (and summers) in the Alps, I’m in a good place to consider everything the prospective American tourist needs to know when planning a trip. With a super El Niño forecasted for the coming season, snow coverage at Alps resorts is likely to be more relevant this year than ever before. Like the Western U.S., seasonal models are forecasting a warm and wet winter for the continent. I’ll take that over a warm and dry winter, but it’s not ideal. Once upon a time, slopes above 1,650 feet were plastered in snow on a regular basis, especially on the northern side of the Alps. Unfortunately, those days are over. That means some lower destinations are far less attractive than they used to be, especially for Americans who usually have to lock in flights and accommodation months in advance. Take Portes du Soleil. With 360 miles of pistes and essentially unlimited off-piste straddling both France and Switzerland, the ski area is one of the world’s largest ski domains. Despite the size, the resort peaks at just 7,200 feet. With base elevations of around 3,300 feet, many storms now bring rain to the lower slopes instead of snow. These days, it’s not uncommon to have rain above 6,500 feet anywhere in the French Alps. Austria is somewhat more continental and protected when warm air surges from the south and west. However, many of its most famous ski resorts sit at relatively low altitudes, and skiing has taken a hit in recent years. Kitzbühel, a big name in ski racing and one of the most famous Austrian resorts for Americans, is ideal in many ways. It embodies European skiing, with a beautiful base village, endless terrain, great après-ski, and a formidable ski history. It’s also on the Ikon Pass. But the resort tops out at just 6,600 feet, with a base elevation of 2,625 feet. Saalbach Skicircus is another legendary Austrian resort, with 168 miles of piste and some of the country’s best off-piste skiing. Epic Pass holders get 5 days here. Nevertheless, with similar elevations to Kitzbühel, the good days, especially off-piste, are more limited than ever. If the weather lines up with a nordstau (European equivalent to Northwest flow bringing in heavy snow) and low snow coverage in Austria, and travel plans are flexible, Americans will love these resorts. But I wouldn’t gamble on booking an overseas trip too far in advance. This is the year to focus on resorts that top out above 10,000 feet in France, Italy, and Switzerland, and above 8,200 feet in Austria. Nearly every American I meet in the Alps has one of two destinations on their itinerary: Chamonix or Zermatt. These towns are burned into the American mountain consciousness, and they’re both on the Ikon Pass, though Chamonix comes with some fine print. But are they worth it? Chamonix is the birthplace of mountaineering. To some extent, it’s also the birthplace of the winter sports industry. The first Winter Olympics were held there in 1924. Chamonix is credited with heralding a new age for dying mountain towns, with a “white gold” rush of winter sports infrastructure throughout the Alps and beyond. There’s clearly history here, but I don’t think that Chamonix is the ideal destination for most Americans looking to head to the Alps for a skiing-focused trip. For starters, the Ikon Pass only includes the Chamonix “Le Pass,” not the Mont-Blanc Unlimited. That’s some annoying fine print that means you can’t ski at the Aiguille du Midi (so no famous Vallée Blanche), Courmayeur (Skyway Monte Bianco), or the top station of the Grands Montets (burned down in 2018 but returning in 2027-’28). Those are the three best things to do when you go to Chamonix. The Unlimited pass is around $80 USD, but like most resorts, prices fluctuate. Instead, “Le Pass” comes with standard access to the five resorts of the Chamonix Valley, which are decent, but not outstanding within the context of the Alps. With Le Pass, the highest access is only 9,186 feet off the Bouchard gondola at the Grands Montets. Getting around between the resorts is punishing during high season. To do the Vallée Blanche or Skyway, you’ll have to splurge an additional 90 Euros ($103 at press time) for a Mont Blanc Unlimited. Meanwhile, Zermatt has long been a stronghold of U.S. tourists. Americans originally discovered Switzerland during vacations after WWII. Today, Zermatt is still full of Americans. For one, it’s on the Ikon Pass. It’s also expensive, but American skiers know how to handle high prices better than most. For some people, waking up with views of the Matterhorn is a bucket list experience. Zermatt is a world-class ski resort with broad, snowsure pistes, fast lifts, and insane views. For the money, however, you can get a less iconic but more quintessential experience in plenty of other places. Though the biggest issue for Zermatt is cost—it feels at least twice as expensive as France—other aspects fall short as well. The food is mediocre compared to France and Italy. The skiing is exposed, cold, and limited on stormy days. Despite being snowsure due to its altitude, Zermatt is not the snowiest place in the Alps. Off-piste is more easily accessible at other resorts. Each Alpine country offers its own blend of culture, pricing, efficiency, access, and more. You’ll have to weigh which factors will make the best vacation for you. France and Italy offer the best food and prices, but you’ll find that things don’t always run as efficiently. Lifts and restaurants may be randomly closed (fermature exceptionelle!), and service isn’t always up to the standard you’d expect in America. In comparison, Switzerland and Austria operate much more efficiently and, generally speaking, receive more snow than France and Italy. Historically, the northern Alps receive the most snow, with resorts like Engelberg and St. Anton tallying the highest numbers. However, signs suggest this climate regime may be changing, and recent years have seen more storms coming from the south. Switzerland and Austria also have the best lifts—most of the existing and planned 3S cable cars in the Alps are here. (The only 3S cable car in North America is Whistler’s Peak2Peak.) In France, and maybe in the world, Tignes/Val d’Isère is the best ski resort for the most people. The skiing offers something for everyone, from toddlers learning to ski to extreme freeriders. The Grand Motte chair accesses glacier terrain at 11,339 feet, the fifth-highest cable car in the Alps. Val d’Isère is a traditional village (culture!), not just a purpose-built ski resort, and the new development is limited to Tignes. Moreover, the base of 5,906 feet is one of the highest for a big resort in the Alps. With about three million American skiers on the Epic and Ikon passes, the only downside is that Tignes/Val d’Isère isn’t included on either—or perhaps that’s a plus, if you’re looking to avoid other Americans. It’s expensive by French standards, but far cheaper than anything you’ll find in Switzerland. Day tickets hover around $80 for adults. Meanwhile, Americans have shifted toward Trois Vallées in recent years. Trois Vallées is one of the best resorts on the Epic Pass—it’s one of the world’s largest, with endless pistes and backcountry terrain alike. Paradiski, consisting of Les Arcs and La Plagne, is another large resort between Trois Vallées and Val d’Isère. Overshadowed by its more famous neighbors, it’s still a fantastic, massive domain with slightly more competitive prices ($66-$85 for adults per day). Most Americans never make it farther south than the Savoie. But that’s precisely where the French Alps begin—at least in a cultural sense. Alpe d’Huez and Les 2 Alpes follow in the tradition of French megaresorts, with mediocre piste offerings but excellent off-piste. However, Serre Chevalier, near the town of Briançon, is the largest and best French resort that most Americans have never heard of. Despite its size, parts of Serre Chevalier still have a village vibe, like Monetier-les-Bains. This hamlet is home to incredible off-piste (the Montagnole) as well as fantastic pistes. The on- and off-mountain dining is also exceptional. Single-day lift tickets are around $78 for adults. Further east, on the border with Italy, is Montgenèvre ($58-$66 for an adult lift ticket). This little gem is located on a pass in the middle of the Alps, and receives snow from both the east and west. It’s also connected with the Via Lattea (see below). Going south, you’ve escaped the land of garish megaresorts and entered into parts unknown—at least for Americans. Abriès and Saint-Véran (both offer lift tickets starting around $48) are two surprisingly high (8,202 feet and 9,186 feet, respectively) resorts in the Queyras, a little-known pocket of the Alps that retains its charm. Hotel La Lobio, not far from Saint-Véran, epitomizes French country lodging and cuisine, run by a single, passionate family. A few valleys further south, Risoul, Vars, Crevoux, and Les Orres are all worthy destinations if the Alps are seeing storms from the southwest. If you’re on the hunt for the best culture—ancient villages and incredible food—and prices in the Alps, Italy should be on your list. The Epic and Ikon passes cover many of the country’s best options. The addition of Aosta Valley to the Ikon Pass means many Americans can now visit magnificent resorts like Monte Rosa, Cervinia, La Thuile, and Courmayeur. Monte Rosa (starting around $80 for a day) is a personal favorite with unlimited off-piste and ski touring from the resort. Consider lodging at some of the smaller base villages, like Alagna (best access) or Gressoney, in the upper Lys Valley. Gressoney-St.-Jean and Gressoney-La-Trinité are home to one of Italy’s few remaining Walser German–speaking populations. Cervino is an alternative to Zermatt. It’s the Italian side of Matterhorn Ski Paradise, which means you can also ski Zermatt. Currently, the crossing is a bit of a bottleneck, with limited-capacity trams serving the Plateau Rosa from the Italian side. However, the 3S cable car, called Cervino The One, is currently under construction and expected to finish by 2030, and will actually make the Klein Matterhorn faster to reach from Cervino than from Zermatt. When you combine that with much better food and prices on the Italian side, Cervino has a lot going for it. South of Aosta, you’ll find the Via Lattea ($80), a collection of several interconnected resorts, the most famous being Sestrière. It’s one of the world’s most vast ski areas, on par with Portes du Soleil and Trois Vallées. It’s not on the megapasses, and I doubt you’ll run into another American. Unfortunately, like Portes du Soleil, altitude is somewhat lacking, though Sestrière reaches 9,186 feet, and these mountains benefit from both easterly and westerly winds. The region’s standout feature is its world-class tree skiing—among the best in the Alps—if conditions allow. The dining is out of this world, even on the mountain. La Marmotta, located on the upper slopes of the Sauze d’Oulx sector, is the best food I’ve ever had on the slopes (38 Euros for a three-course meal and wine, and that’s expensive for Italy). And I’ve eaten at a lot of restaurants in the Alps. Try staying at Agriturismo Barba Gust for the most authentic Alpine ski experience you can get. The Dolomites have had the spotlight over the past year thanks to the Cortina Olympics. The Dolomiti Superski ($98), on Ikon, is still a great option for Americans—perhaps the best option in the country. These resorts don’t get the most snow, but the natural scenery of the Dolomites sets them apart from other resorts in the Alps. Because this is a collection of relatively small ski resorts, you’ll find many authentic villages rather than manufactured ski bases. Cortina is the most famous (and luxurious), but Val Gardena, Kronplatz, and Alta Badia are better for pure skiing. Like many resorts in Italy, the on-mountain dining is unreal—Baita Ciadinat, on the upper slopes of Val Gardena, is a must. Austria is a country whose national identity revolves around skiing. In fact, no country in the world has better slopes and access. The Austrian Alps are full of large, efficient ski resorts that combine high annual snowfall and medium prices—maybe just a bit more expensive than France but much less than Switzerland (and the U.S.). Austria is well-represented on the Epic and Ikon passes. While the days of unlimited fresh tracks are long gone at any resort, Austrian ski culture still tends a bit more toward the pistes. Therefore, you can often find that fresh tracks last longer here, especially on snowy days—Austrians don’t seem to like storm skiing. Austria is also holding down the après fort at a time when interest in après seems to be diminishing in the rest of the Alps. If you like loud, commercial dance music and general debauchery after a day of skiing, you’re going to want to focus your vacation search on Austria. The Epic Pass offers more in Austria than the Ikon Pass. However, Epic Pass holders receive five consecutive days at Skicircus Saalbach, Sölden, Zillertal, and Silveretta Montafon, all world-class resorts. So you could do nearly a month in Austria with the Epic, with access to close to 1,000 kms (620 miles) of pistes, several glaciers, and endless off-piste and ski touring. In my opinion, . It’s on the edge of the Alps’ most consistent snowbelt and has extensive off-piste terrain. The place is enormous, whether you want to ski on- or off-piste. Unfortunately for Americans, the Epic Pass has some fine print (you only get three consecutive days, and you have to stay at one of a few participating hotels to redeem them). In my opinion, Ski Arlberg (St. Anton) is still the gold standard of Austrian skiing. It’s on the edge of the Alps’ most consistent snowbelt and has extensive off-piste terrain. The Ikon Pass is a bit less fruitful. Ischgl ($80-$95) is a fantastic all-around resort, if a bit devoid of character. It’s also connected to Samnaun in Switzerland. Kitzbühel ($80-$93) is Austria’s signature resort, though as I mentioned earlier, its appeal as an international destination is getting hampered by its lack of altitude (same with Saalbach). I always recommend Americans check out Innsbruck. It’s a real city, offering the same benefits as the great capitals of Europe, like palaces and universities. Over 100,000 locals live here, not just an endless stream of tourists. The local resort of Nordkette is nothing to write home about, but you can easily access a dozen or so resorts on the Innsbruck Pass ($185 for a two-day pass), from low elevation all the way up to the Stubai Glacier. The city also has excellent shuttle and rail transport so that you can get anywhere in an hour. St. Anton? An hour west by train. Kitzbühel and Saalbach? An hour east by train. Austria has over 400 ski resorts, so there are plenty of secret gems to discover. Just keep an eye on the weather. Often, a ridge can set up over western Europe and keep most of the Alps dry. However, sometimes moisture can flow from the north along the backside of this ridge and make a direct hit on the eastern Austrian Alps, east of Salzburg. Resorts like Zauchensee ($86) and Obertauern ($82) are great options, and you’ll see far fewer tourists (and probably zero Americans). One of Switzerland’s biggest successes is the abundance of carless base villages. Zermatt is famous for its Gornergrat railway, but there are dozens of car-free villages, including Wengen, Saas-Fee, and Mürren. For me, though it may seem like a small detail, the absence of cars goes a long way toward making you feel as if you’d gone back in time. And that’s more valuable than ever these days. Switzerland is also the most snowsure region of the Alps, with plenty of high-altitude, north-facing slopes along the range’s north side. There’s a reason the largest glaciers in the Alps are here. The ski resorts are cozier and more specialized, which can be a pro or a con, depending on what you’re looking for. There are a few exceptions to the cozyness. Verbier ($100), one of the most well-known resorts to Americans, sprawls across four valleys and offers up some of the Alps’ most “big mountain” terrain. However, if you’re looking to ski off-piste, Verbier is home to all the most ambitious freeriders in Europe, who will snag your line before you even know it exists. By the time you figure out the lay of the land, these young guns will already be at work cooking your lunch. You’re better off going to Austria. In place of Zermatt, Americans should consider Saas Fee ($102). Like Zermatt, it’s a car-free village, but it’s much more authentic. Most chalets are hundreds of years old. The top funicular reaches 11,482 feet, though the variety of pistes does not match Zermatt. However, Saas Fee truly embodies the Swiss Valais, the canton home to Zermatt, Verbier, and other famous resorts. Andermatt ($100-$120) and Engelberg ($80-$90) are both top off-piste destinations. Unfortunately, they both only have one lift that accesses the summit, which means skier capacity is low, lift lines are long, and the limited terrain gets claimed in the blink of an eye. Laax ($47-$150) and Arosa Lenzerheide ($108) are larger resorts that are less known for their freeride offerings; however, they have more efficient lifts and fewer hungry freeriders to compete with. If you can afford it, Davos ($97-$113) and St. Moritz ($67) are also quite good for off-piste skiing, despite their reputation as luxury resorts (St. Moritz is on the Ikon Pass). Switzerland has just 23 million skier visits a year, despite having over 300 ski resorts. That’s about 100 more resorts than France, which clocks in at 51 million visits. The result is, outside of Verbier and Zermatt, a less crowded experience. Just know that it will cost you double compared to the other Alpine countries.

The Prisma monitor uses an LG IPS Black panel with a 5120 × 2160 resolution (5K), providing decent horizontal workspace for demanding applications. Its integrated docking station, expandable storage, wireless charging and dedicated computer cradle are intended to reduce the number of separate desktop accessories. A 5K ultrawide display with integrated storage and connectivity The MP Prisma has a 40-inch curved screen that supports a 120Hz refresh rate, alongside a quasi-10-bit colour reproduction capable of displaying about 1.07 billion colours. With 99% DCI-P3 coverage, the display also accommodates colour-sensitive applications, including photo editing, video production and other professional creative workloads. The integrated docking station supports USB-C, USB-A and USB-B connections, alongside dedicated SD and microSD readers for transferring files between devices. An onboard KVM switch allows two connected computers to share peripherals, while Picture-by-Picture functionality simultaneously displays their respective outputs on screen. This 5K monitor also incorporates an M.2 SSD expansion slot, allowing users to install additional storage without requiring an external enclosure. Mac mini cradle, wireless charging and crowdfunding concerns A dedicated cradle integrated into Prisma's supporting structure accommodates Apple's Mac mini and Mac Studio computers, keeping their enclosures off the desktop. It also incorporates an active cooling fan that adjusts its operation according to temperature, although detailed thermal performance figures remain unavailable. Laptop users can charge their devices with the USB-C port, potentially reducing the number of separate power connections required in everyday use. A 15W wireless charging pad occupies the monitor's base area, providing a dedicated charging location for compatible smartphones without additional desktop accessories. The display also features a retractable iPhone mounting mechanism that supports Apple's Continuity Camera functionality, including Center Stage and Desk View. Though it comes with a docking station for Mac Studio and Mac Mini, Prisma also supports Windows laptops, PCs, and other devices using its connectivity options. The Prisma monitor is available through Kickstarter for $999 under a limited introductory offer, representing a 38% discount against its $1,600 retail price. item.title: SALES: Apple fan wants to convince 'Cheesegreater' Mac Pro owners to spend $500 on a 'conversion kit' to 'replace the proprietary platform with standard upgradable PC hardware'
item.description:
Source: Latest from TechRadar US in News
- The kit adapts Apple's 2019 Mac Pro case for standard PC parts - Buyers must source the motherboard, processor, graphics card, memory, and power supply - The original fans and front controls can remain in service An enthusiast is seeking crowdfunding support for a conversion system that would let owners reuse Apple's 2019 Mac Pro enclosure with conventional desktop PC components. The proposed kit accommodates standard motherboards, power supplies and graphics cards while retaining the aluminium chassis, original cooling fans and front controls. However, the campaign on Kickstarter has attracted just $7 from one backer against its $10,686 funding goal, with 28 days remaining. Replacing Apple's internal hardware without sacrificing its design Known as the Cheesegrater because of its perforated aluminium exterior, the Mac Pro 7,1 has a case that owners can reuse for a new PC The kit replaces Apple's original internal hardware with parts that allow users to install standard PC components inside the existing case. It supports ATX motherboards, standard power supplies, and graphics cards up to 308 mm long and 140 mm tall. Users can install air coolers up to 140 mm tall or liquid cooling systems with radiators up to 240 mm long. The kit also provides space for two SATA storage drives, each measuring 2.5 or 3.5 inches, and is designed to retain Apple's three original front fans through three custom adapter circuit boards and associated wiring. A dedicated interface also connects the original power button, indicator light, and two USB-C ports supporting USB 3.1 Gen 1. The planned package includes a motherboard and power supply mounting plate, two drive sleds, two drive cables, custom circuit boards, fasteners, and an internal power cable. It will also include a bracket for the motherboard's rear connections and expansion slots, while an optional processor cooling cover costs extra. The conversion kit is expected to cost around $500, but buyers must pay separately for the Mac Pro case and the PC components installed inside it. These include the motherboard, processor, graphics card, memory, power supply, storage drives and cooling system, which could raise the total cost considerably. The kit is designed to retain the Mac Pro's original three front fans, power button, indicator light and two USB-C ports. Special adapters help connect the original fans, while another electronic component keeps the front controls and ports working with the replacement PC hardware. Installing the kit requires removing the Mac Pro's original internal components, fitting the replacement parts and connecting wires. The installation can only be done properly by experienced PC builders, though the kit includes a guide for fitting the new components into the Mac Pro case. After conversion, the original chassis remains the same, allowing owners to reverse the conversion if they later want to reinstall Apple's hardware. However, buyers must check their graphics card's dimensions, available cooling space, and compatibility with the motherboard before purchasing the kit. item.title: SALES: 10 Best Winter Backpacking and Mountaineering Packs
item.description:
Source: Sectionhiker.com
Winter Backpacking Packs are more specialized than regular three-season backpacks, with a stronger emphasis on carrying heavier loads, external attachment points, and durability for handling bulky gear with sharp points, such as snowshoes, skis, ice axes, and crampons. They also favor more pockets and quick access and stowage, so you can avoid standing around between gear transitions and getting cold. Pack volumes range from 50L to 80L. Here are our picks for the best winter backpacking backpacks: Backpacks tailored for mountaineering and winter backpacking use have a different feature set than most 3 season packs. Below are the features I’ve found most useful for winter trips in mountainous terrain. While I think these translate fairly broadly across winter locales, you need to judge which features are most relevant to your needs. If you plan on taking weekend-length cold-weather trips, you’ll probably want a pack with 55-80 liters of internal capacity. The sweet spot is approximately 70 liters, but you may be able to reduce it to as low as 50 liters if you carry less gear or require less insulation. Choose a pack with adequate compression so you can shrink its volume when you don’t need it, while keeping the empty pack under 5 pounds. Pack and gear weight matters even more in winter than at other times of the year because you’ll be wearing and carrying more of it. Mountaineering and winter backpacking packs need multiple external attachment points to carry sharp, pointy, or bulky gear (microspikes, crampons, shovels, and snowshoes) that won’t fit in the pack’s main storage compartments. The most useful external attachment points include compression straps, daisy chains, hip belt webbing or gear loops, and ice ax loops with shaft holders. Compression straps serve two purposes: to help compress a load and bring the weight closer to your core muscles, where it can be carried more easily; and to attach sleeping pads, snowshoes, avalanche shovels, or skis to the sides of your pack instead of the front, so that the load doesn’t pull you backward and off-balance. When choosing a backpack, look for ones with two or three tiers of compression straps that run horizontally across the sides of the pack. The compression straps should be adjustable and easy to undo while wearing gloves, so you can slide winter tools under them. Avoid packs with compression straps that zig-zag back and forth across the pack, using one strap to save weight. These are very difficult to use, especially when wearing gloves. Daisy chains are often sewn onto mountaineering and winter packs and can be used to lash extra gear to the back or sides of the pack using canvas or Velcro straps. They usually have many loops sewn into them that run the length of your pack from top to bottom. There are two kinds of ice axes in this world – straight walking axes and curved climbing axes. If you need to carry a walking ax, look for a pack with at least one ice ax loop at the base and a shaft holder, both off-center on the back. The shaft holder can be a simple cord lock like those found on many Osprey packs, or a more robust buckle. If you plan on carrying two climbing axes, look for packs with two ice ax loops and shaft holders. Some climbing-oriented packs feature canvas or plastic gear loops on the outside of the hip belt, allowing you to clip climbing carabiners to them. While not a substitute for a proper sit-harness, these loops can be quite convenient for racking climbing gear. Crampon pockets offer a convenient, safe place to store crampons when you’re not wearing them. Located on the side of the pack farthest from you, they keep the crampon points away from your arms, legs, head, and gear, where they can do real damage. In winter, a backpack that can expand in volume to carry more gear can be very helpful. One way to do this is to buy a pack with a floating lid, typically featuring a top pocket that can detach from the main body of the pack but remains secured by four straps. In this way, you can sandwich extra gear, like a coil of rope, between the pocket and the top of your pack. Zipper access to the front or side of the backpack is a highly desirable feature for winter use because it makes for much faster stops, eliminating the need to pop open a top lid and dig around your backpack looking for gear. You don’t want to stand around for very long on winter trips, but to get moving so your body can generate heat to stay warm. SectionHiker never accepts payment for gear reviews or editorial coverage. item.title: SALES: Always late for meetings or failing at life goals? This affordable planning app was made for you
item.description:
Source: Latest from TechRadar US in News
How long has it been since you used a paper diary? 10 years, 15, maybe even 20. Can you remember the year it was or the brand of diary? Was it when you were in school, and you had to write down your homework? Long gone for me. Or was it your first job, and you used a Filofax to keep track of your meetings and action points? Or maybe you still use one to keep a note of everyone’s birthdays. For me, there’s something strangely nostalgic and surprisingly grounding about flicking through a paper planner. I remember buying a new one each year, around Christmastime or January, if I’d completely failed at staying organized. Being able to discard an older diary and embrace a fresh one felt like a new start, a moment to turn my back on the difficulties of the previous year and embrace the opportunities ahead. But it’s no surprise that digital diaries and online planning tools have made paper alternatives all but obsolete. Digital apps are available 24/7 on any device and have more features than you can shake a stick at. I think that’s a little bit of a shame, but one app trying to bring together paper and digital planning is Ultimate Planner. This is part of a regular series of articles exploring the apps that we couldn't live without. Read them all here. Okay, Ultimate Planner is still a digital tool (sorry), but it replicates the paper diary experience in ways that I’ve never seen before. With paper diary-inspired layouts, Filofax-esque tabs, and stylus compatibility, it’s as close to a paper diary as you’re ever going to get without actually going to the shops and buying one. Ultimate Planner, according to its creators, is “the most customizable digital planner app" available. And after just five minutes of use, you’ll probably be inclined to agree. With it, you can plan your day, organize tasks and actions, manage goals, and even track habits. The journey begins by picking a planner type. Your choice customizes the features, tabs, and tools you access. If you choose ‘Ultimate Planner,' as I did, then you’ll be able to use everything the app has to offer without restriction. Just a word of warning: things can get pretty complex and overwhelming if you choose to show every single feature. If you have a specific type of planner in mind related to teaching, gratitude, or business, for example, then you can choose one of those instead. Just note that these additional options require a Pro account, which costs $39.99 / £39.99 per year or a $69.99 / £69.99 one-off charge for lifetime access. Unfortunately, there’s no free trial, although you can access the core features with a free account. Unlimited customization is a core part of the app’s raison d'être. Being able to customize layouts with bespoke sections means you can create a planner that matches your specific workflow. You can even choose from numerous templates to get an aesthetic that feels personal and inspiring. The reality is that with all the feature permutations, Ultimate Planner is far from a one-size-fits-all app. Unlimited Planner also just keeps going. When one year is done, another year seamlessly rolls around. That means you have access to unlimited pages, notebooks, and planning layouts. With the Pro version, there’s no limit on the number of planners you can create, so why not use it for both work and personal reasons? That’ll certainly make the very most of the subscription cost. The Ultimate Planner might look, for all intents and purposes, like a paper planner, but it’s also able to sync seamlessly with one or more of your digital calendars. This is an ideal solution for tracking events and managing tasks right alongside all your other planning notes and tables. Within each synced calendar account, you can choose which specific calendars you wish to display. This is ideal for work accounts, which might contain multiple people’s calendars. You can also rest assured that your data will be perfectly synced across a range of platforms and devices, including iPad, iPhone, Android, and web. I’ve loved being able to access the planner on my phone on the go and then pick up where I left off when I’m sat at my desk. Having everything in one place, connected to all my devices, keeps me on track and organized. Download Ultimate Planner on iOS and Android.
